title: How Long Does a Luxury Remodel Take in Los Angeles? A Realistic Timeline
meta_description: A realistic timeline for a Los Angeles luxury remodel and resale: due diligence, design, permits and plan check, construction, listing and closing.
author: Oliver Thornton
body_html:
Time is one of the biggest variables in a luxury remodel. Every month adds interest, taxes and insurance, and a project that runs long can lose much of its margin even if the home sells at the expected price. Here is what a realistic timeline looks like in Los Angeles, phase by phase.

The Phases

PhaseWhat happensTypical range
Due diligence and escrowInspections, zoning and floor-area check, contractor walk-through2–6 weeks
DesignPlans, engineering, finish selections1–3 months
Permits and plan checkSubmission, corrections, permit issuance2–6 months
ConstructionDemolition through final inspection6–12 months
Prep and listingStaging, photography, launch2–4 weeks
Marketing and escrowShowings, offers, closing1–3 months

These are general ranges, not commitments. Scope, the building department’s workload and market conditions all move them.

Overlap Is How Time Is Saved

Experienced teams don’t run phases strictly one after another. Design often starts during escrow, long-lead items like windows and doors are ordered as soon as plans are set, and listing preparation begins before final inspection. The difference between a 14-month and a 22-month project is often how well phases overlap.

What Stretches a Schedule

  • Plan-check corrections that send drawings back for another round
  • Existing conditions found once walls and floors are opened; see hidden costs in a luxury remodel
  • Long-lead materials such as custom windows, doors and appliances
  • Hillside requirements such as geology reports and grading approvals
  • Inspection scheduling and utility coordination near the end

Remodel vs. Ground-Up

A remodel that keeps part of the existing structure usually moves faster than new construction, because it often avoids separate entitlement and carries a smaller scope. That is a big part of why we favor remodel-first projects; see remodel vs. new construction.

Frequently Asked Questions

How long does a luxury remodel take in Los Angeles?
From purchase to resale, many well-run remodel and expansion projects take roughly 12 to 24 months, depending on scope, permitting and the market. Larger or hillside projects can take longer.

Do remodels need permits in Los Angeles?
Yes. Structural, electrical, plumbing, mechanical and most layout changes require building permits and inspections. Many remodels need no separate entitlement approval, which keeps the timeline shorter than new construction.

What slows a remodel down most?
Plan-check corrections, scope surprises once walls are opened, long-lead materials, and inspection scheduling.

Can work start before permits are issued?
Some non-structural work, such as interior demolition, may be possible with the right permits, but most construction must wait for permit issuance.

title: Beverly Hills, the South Bay and Orange County: Luxury Markets Outside Measure ULA
meta_description: Why luxury developers look at Beverly Hills, the South Bay and Orange County: no Measure ULA, strong resale liquidity, and what changes when buying outside LA.
author: Oliver Thornton
body_html:
Measure ULA changed the math for high-end development inside the City of Los Angeles. For developers who still want to build and sell above the threshold, a set of nearby markets outside city limits has become more attractive: Beverly Hills proper, the South Bay and parts of Orange County.

Why These Markets

  • No Measure ULA. Sales outside City of Los Angeles limits aren’t subject to it, so a higher finished price doesn’t hit the same tax cliff. Other local transfer taxes may still apply.
  • Deep luxury demand. These markets have established buyer pools for high-end homes and above-average resale liquidity.
  • Strong fundamentals. Schools, beaches, employment centers and limited new supply support values.

How the Markets Differ

MarketWhat draws buyersWhat to watch
Beverly Hills properGlobal name recognition, flat streets, top-tier price levelsThe city’s own design review and building standards
South BayBeach cities, schools, family demandCoastal-zone permits on some sites; city-specific rules
Select Orange CountyCoastal and master-planned luxury communitiesHOA and community design approvals in some areas

What Changes When You Leave the City

Every city writes its own zoning, floor-area rules, design review and permitting process. A strategy that works on a Westside street in the City of Los Angeles may need a different scope, timeline or design in Beverly Hills or a beach city. That is why these markets need local diligence on every site, and why we pass on sites that require design review boards or Coastal Commission approval.

Where This Fits Our Buy Box

In the City of Los Angeles, we generally price luxury acquisitions so the finished home sells below the Measure ULA threshold. Outside the city, in Beverly Hills proper and select Orange County and South Bay markets, we consider higher purchase prices where resale liquidity supports them. If you have a property in one of these markets, see our luxury buy box.

Transfer taxes and local rules vary and change; confirm the requirements for a specific property with qualified professionals.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does Measure ULA apply in Beverly Hills?
No. Measure ULA applies only to sales within City of Los Angeles limits. Beverly Hills is a separate city.

Do South Bay and Orange County cities have their own transfer taxes?
Transfer taxes vary by city and county. Buyers and sellers should confirm the taxes that apply to a specific property before pricing a sale.

Why consider higher price points outside the City of Los Angeles?
Without Measure ULA, a higher finished price doesn't trigger the same transfer tax cliff, and some of these markets have deep, liquid luxury demand.

Are the rules different outside the City of Los Angeles?
Yes. Each city has its own zoning, floor-area limits, design review and permitting process, so every market needs its own local diligence.

title: Pricing, Staging and Launch: How Luxury Flips Sell in Los Angeles
meta_description: How a finished luxury remodel goes to market in Los Angeles: pricing to closed comparables, staging, photography, launch timing and Measure ULA price points.
author: Oliver Thornton
body_html:
A beautifully finished home still has to sell, and how it goes to market can matter as much as how it was built. The first few weeks set the tone: a home that launches at the right price, looking its best, usually sells faster and closer to asking than one that has to chase the market down.

Price to the Closed Comparables

The list price should come from recent closed sales of comparable finished homes, the same comparables used in underwriting, adjusted for size, lot, street and finish level. Overpricing to “leave room to negotiate” often backfires: the home sits, buyers notice the days on market, and the eventual price can end up lower.

Presentation

ElementWhy it matters
StagingShows scale and how rooms live, especially open plans and primary suites
Photography and videoMost buyers first see the home online
Landscaping and entryCurb appeal sets the first impression in person and in photos
Twilight and lifestyle shotsHighlight lighting design, indoor-outdoor living and views
Disclosures readyPermits and reports available up front build buyer confidence

Launch Timing

Spring is traditionally the strongest season, but a well-priced home can sell year-round. More important than the month is a strong launch: everything ready on day one, broad agent outreach before the first weekend, and a clear offer process.

The Measure ULA Price Line

In the City of Los Angeles, the Measure ULA transfer tax applies to the full price once a sale crosses the threshold. A home near that line often prices just below it, because a sale just above can net the seller less. Planning for that starts at acquisition, not at listing.

Working With the Brokerage

Having the listing agent involved from design onward helps align the finished home with what local buyers want and how comparable homes are being marketed. The principals’ brokerage relationships are part of how we plan each exit before we buy.

Frequently Asked Questions

How should a finished flip be priced?
Against recent closed sales of comparable finished homes, adjusted for size, lot, street and finish level, rather than against hoped-for values or the highest active listings.

Is staging worth it for a luxury home?
Usually. Staging and professional photography help buyers understand scale and lifestyle, and most buyers first see a home online.

When is the best time to list in Los Angeles?
Spring is traditionally strong, but a well-priced, well-presented home can sell in any season. Avoiding major holidays usually helps.

How does Measure ULA affect pricing?
In the City of Los Angeles, pricing just above the threshold can net the seller less than pricing just below it, so the threshold often shapes the list price.

title: Hollywood Hills vs. the Westside: Two Luxury Markets, Two Playbooks
meta_description: How luxury remodels differ in the Hollywood Hills and on the Westside: buyers, lots, views, construction costs, timelines and what makes each market work.
author: Oliver Thornton
body_html:
The Hollywood Hills and the Westside are both premier luxury markets, but a remodel that wins in one can struggle in the other. The buyers, the lots, the construction and the timeline are all different. Experienced developers run a different playbook in each.

Side by Side

Hollywood HillsWestside flats
What buyers pay forViews, privacy, architecture, indoor-outdoor livingSchools, walkability, space, beach and job access
Typical lotsSloped, irregular, sometimes narrow streetsFlat, regular, easier access
ConstructionFoundations, retaining and access can add costGenerally simpler and more predictable
RulesHillside floor-area and grading limits, fire-zone standardsFlatland floor-area limits; fewer site constraints
TimelineOften longerOften shorter

What Works in the Hills

The best Hills projects pair an exceptional view with a naturally flat building pad, privacy from neighbors and a design buyers can’t find elsewhere. Steep sites that need heavy retaining or caissons, or homes stacked three or more levels down a slope, carry costs that land before any buyer sees them. See hillside development costs.

What Works on the Westside

On the flats, the opportunity is usually space: an under-improved house on a good street with room to add a primary suite, bedrooms and indoor-outdoor living. Construction is more predictable, and demand from families and professionals is deep. See adding square footage.

The Common Thread

In both markets, the deal is made at purchase: buying a home whose finished value is supported by closed comparables, with a scope that fits the street and a timeline that fits the budget. The principals built their record in both, and we look for remodel-first opportunities in Class A, A− and B+ neighborhoods across them.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is it more expensive to remodel in the Hollywood Hills?
Often, yes. Hillside sites can bring foundation, retaining, access and fire-zone requirements that flat Westside lots usually don't.

Who buys luxury homes in the Hollywood Hills?
Often buyers who prioritize views, privacy and architecture, including entertainment-industry and creative-industry buyers.

Who buys on the Westside?
Often families and professionals who prioritize schools, walkability, beaches and access to Westside job centers.

Which market is better for a flip?
Neither is better in general. The Westside often offers simpler construction and deep demand; the Hills can reward exceptional view properties with strong prices.

title: Hidden Costs in a Los Angeles Luxury Remodel
meta_description: The costs that surprise luxury remodel budgets in Los Angeles: foundations, sewer lines, electrical service, drainage, permits, energy code and carrying costs.
author: Oliver Thornton
body_html:
Most remodel budgets don’t fail on finishes. They fail on what is behind the walls, under the floor and at the edge of the property. Older Los Angeles homes in particular can hide expensive conditions that only appear once work begins. Knowing where to look is half of budgeting well.

Where Surprises Usually Come From

ItemWhy it adds costHow to check early
FoundationCracking, settlement or undersized footings, especially with additionsStructural inspection before closing
Sewer lateralRoot intrusion, cracked clay pipe, or a required replacementCamera inspection
Electrical serviceOlder panels and service sized well below modern needsElectrician review of panel and service
PlumbingGalvanized or deteriorated supply and drain linesPlumber inspection
Drainage and gradingWater against the foundation or poor site drainageSite walk after rain, grading review
FramingRot, termite damage or prior unpermitted workPest and general inspection
Code upgradesEnergy, fire and accessibility requirements triggered by the scopeEarly review with the designer

Soft Costs That Add Up

  • Permit, plan-check and school fees
  • Engineering, surveys and soils reports
  • Utility connection and upgrade fees
  • Insurance during construction
  • Carrying costs: interest, property taxes and utilities for the full hold

Unpermitted Work

Older homes often carry past additions or conversions that were never permitted. Bringing them up to code, or removing them, can change both the budget and the schedule. Comparing the home to its permit history before closing avoids a surprise during plan check.

Budgeting for the Unknown

The practical answer is inspections before closing and a real contingency in the budget, sized to the home’s age and the scope. A remodel without contingency is a remodel that will run over. See how a luxury fix-and-flip is underwritten.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the most common surprise cost in an older LA home?
Foundation, plumbing and electrical issues that only become visible once walls and floors are opened are among the most common.

Should I inspect the sewer line before buying?
A camera inspection of the sewer lateral is a common step for older homes, since repairing or replacing it can be costly.

Why do electrical upgrades come up so often?
Modern kitchens, HVAC, EV chargers and added square footage often require more electrical capacity than an older home's service provides.

How much contingency is enough?
It depends on the home's age and condition and the scope of work. Older homes and larger scopes generally need more contingency.

title: What Makes a Neighborhood Class A, A− or B+?
meta_description: What developers mean by Class A, A- and B+ neighborhoods: price levels, buyer demand, liquidity, schools and housing stock, and why it matters for resale.
author: Oliver Thornton
body_html:
Developers and investors often describe neighborhoods with letter grades: Class A, A−, B+ and so on. It isn’t an official system, and every firm draws the lines a little differently, but it is useful shorthand for one practical question: how confident can you be that a finished home will sell, and at what price?

What the Grades Usually Mean

GradeTypical characteristics
Class AEstablished, high-demand neighborhoods with top price levels, strong schools and consistently fast resale
Class A−Very desirable areas just below the top tier, often with slightly older housing stock or less consistent pricing
Class B+Solid, improving neighborhoods with good demand and room for prices to grow
Below B+Thinner buyer demand, more price sensitivity, longer time on market

The Signals That Matter

  • Resale liquidity: how many comparable homes sell, and how fast
  • Price level and trend: recent closed prices for finished homes
  • Owner-occupancy: neighborhoods of owners tend to hold value
  • Schools and amenities: walkability, parks, retail and dining
  • Access: proximity to job centers and transit
  • Housing stock: a mix of updated and under-improved homes signals opportunity

Why We Focus on A, A− and B+

For a remodel and resale, the biggest risk is a finished home that doesn’t sell, or sells only after long, expensive months on the market. Deep buyer demand reduces that risk. That is why our luxury buy box focuses on Class A, A− and B+ neighborhoods, Westside first, with select hillside, Beverly Hills, Orange County and South Bay opportunities.

Block by Block

Grades describe neighborhoods, but value is set block by block. A busy street, a commercial edge or a steep, narrow road can put a house in a lower comparable set than the neighborhood average. Experienced local operators underwrite the street, not just the zip code.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is neighborhood class an official rating?
No. It is informal shorthand used by investors and developers to describe relative quality, demand and price level. Different firms define it differently.

Why do developers focus on Class A, A- and B+ areas?
Those areas tend to have deeper buyer demand and more consistent resale, which reduces the risk that a finished home sits unsold.

Can a B+ neighborhood be a better investment than Class A?
Sometimes. B+ areas can offer lower purchase prices with improving demand, while Class A areas can have higher prices and thinner margins.

What signals neighborhood quality?
Recent sale prices and how quickly homes sell, school quality, owner-occupancy, walkability and access to job centers, and the condition of the surrounding housing.

title: Selling Your Home to a Luxury Developer: What Owners and Agents Should Know
meta_description: What luxury developers look for in a dated Los Angeles home, how they price it, what to expect from an as-is sale, and what to send for a fast answer.
author: Oliver Thornton
body_html:
Not every house is best sold to a family who will move in tomorrow. A dated home on a strong street, especially one with room to grow, is often worth more to a developer who plans to remodel and expand it. This guide explains how that sale works for owners, estates and listing agents.

What Luxury Developers Look For

  • Location: Class A, A− and B+ neighborhoods; see what those grades mean
  • An under-improved house: dated finishes or layout relative to the street
  • Room to grow: unused floor area or an expandable footprint
  • A simple path: no design review board, historic overlay or coastal permit
  • Hillside, selectively: exceptional views with flat building area

How Developers Price It

A developer works backward from the expected sale price of the finished home, then subtracts design, construction, carrying, financing and selling costs, plus a margin for risk. Homes with clear upside and a simple scope support the strongest offers. In the City of Los Angeles, the Measure ULA threshold also shapes what a developer can pay.

Why Owners Sell to Developers

BenefitWhat it means
As-is saleNo repairs, staging or open houses
CertaintyA buyer who has already underwritten the property
Flexible timingClosings arranged around estates, moves or trusts
SpeedCash or private financing when the deal calls for it

What to Send for a Fast Answer

  • Address and asking price
  • Bedrooms, bathrooms, home size and lot size
  • Photos, and any known issues or past permits
  • Occupancy and preferred timing

We reply within two business days with a yes, a no, or our questions, and honor agent commissions. See our luxury buy box or submit a property.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do I need to fix up my home before selling to a developer?
No. Developers buy as-is and plan to renovate, so repairs and staging generally aren't needed.

How do developers price an under-improved home?
They work backward from the expected sale price of the finished home, then subtract renovation, carrying, selling and financing costs, plus a margin for risk.

Do you work with listing agents?
Yes. Assemble Capital works with listing and buyer's agents and honors the agreed commission.

What kinds of homes are a fit?
Under-improved single-family homes in Class A, A- and B+ neighborhoods, ideally with room to add square footage, typically purchased between $1,000,000 and $3,000,000, with higher prices considered outside the City of Los Angeles.

title: How a Luxury Fix-and-Flip Is Underwritten in Los Angeles
meta_description: How experienced developers underwrite a Los Angeles luxury fix-and-flip: closed comparables, resale value, scope, carrying costs, contingency and exit timing.
author: Oliver Thornton
body_html:
A luxury fix-and-flip looks simple from the outside: buy an under-improved house, renovate it beautifully, sell it for more. The difference between a good project and a painful one is decided before closing, in the underwriting. This is how experienced developers approach it in Los Angeles, in general terms.

Start With the Exit

Underwriting begins with what the finished home will sell for, its after-repair value. That number comes from recent closed sales of comparable finished homes nearby: similar size, bedrooms, lot, street quality and finish level. Listings and appreciation forecasts are not part of the base case. If the project only works because prices rise, it is a bet on the market, not a plan.

The Numbers That Matter

LineWhat goes into it
Purchase pricePlus closing costs and any seller credits
Design and permitsArchitect, engineering, permit fees, surveys and reports
ConstructionHard costs for the full scope, priced by the builder
ContingencyA reserve for what the walls reveal
Carrying costsInterest, taxes, insurance and utilities for the full hold
Selling costsCommissions, transfer taxes, staging and escrow
Resale valueClosed comparable sales of finished homes

Scope Is Where Risk Hides

Older Los Angeles houses keep their secrets until the walls are open: foundations, framing, plumbing, electrical and drainage. A careful scope, inspections before closing and a realistic contingency are what keep a remodel on budget. Projects that keep part of the existing structure can often be permitted and financed as remodels; see remodel vs. new construction.

Time Is a Cost

Every month of design, permitting, construction and marketing adds interest, taxes and insurance. A schedule that slips by a few months can erase much of a project’s margin even if the sale price is right. That is why we favor short, defined scopes and price-point discipline over open-ended rebuilds.

Price-Point Discipline

In the City of Los Angeles, a finished home that sells just above the Measure ULA threshold can net less than one that sells just below it. Underwriting a luxury flip in the city now means deciding the target resale price first and fitting the scope to it.

The Downside Case

Good underwriting asks what happens if the home sells for less, takes longer to sell, or costs more to build, and whether the project still works. If a modest miss on any one of those turns the project upside down, it is too thin.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is ARV in a fix-and-flip?
After-repair value: the estimated sale price of the home once the remodel is complete, based on recent closed sales of comparable finished homes.

Why underwrite to closed sales instead of listings?
Closed sales show what buyers actually paid. Listing prices show what sellers hope to get, and can overstate value.

How much contingency should a remodel carry?
It depends on the age, condition and scope of the house, but remodels generally need more contingency than new construction because existing conditions are only fully visible once walls are opened.

Why does time matter so much on a flip?
Every month adds interest, taxes, insurance and utilities. A longer schedule can erode a project's margin even if the finished home sells at the expected price.

title: Finishes That Sell: Designing a Remodel for Westside Buyers
meta_description: The design choices that help a Los Angeles luxury remodel sell: layout, light, kitchens, primary suites, indoor-outdoor living and avoiding over-improvement.
author: Oliver Thornton
body_html:
The same square footage can sell very differently depending on how it is laid out and finished. For a luxury remodel on the Westside or in the Hills, design is not decoration; it is how the project reaches its sale price in a reasonable time.

Layout Before Finishes

Buyers notice flow, light and ceiling height before they notice tile. Opening the kitchen to the family room, creating sightlines to the yard, and adding a true primary suite usually do more for value than any single finish choice. Get the plan right first.

Where to Spend

AreaWhy it matters
KitchenThe center of the home; buyers expect quality appliances, storage and an island
Primary suiteSpacious bedroom, spa-like bath and real closet space
Indoor-outdoor livingLarge openings to a deck, yard or pool, central to Los Angeles living
Natural lightWindows, skylights and taller ceilings change how a home feels
Curb appealLandscaping, entry and exterior materials shape the first impression

Where to Hold Back

  • Finishes far beyond what comparable homes offer
  • Highly personal or trend-driven choices
  • Custom features that add cost without changing the comparable set
  • Scope that extends the schedule more than it adds value

Design for the Comparable Set

The right finish level is the one that wins against the homes a buyer will compare it to. That is why remodel design starts with the same closed comparable sales the underwriting uses: what finished homes on similar streets offer, and what buyers paid for them.

Durable Over Trendy

Warm natural materials, a restrained palette and quality fixtures tend to photograph well, show well and age well. A home that looks current for years, not just for the listing, serves both the buyer and the developer’s reputation.

Frequently Asked Questions

Which rooms matter most to luxury buyers?
Kitchens, primary suites and the main living area, especially when they open to usable outdoor space.

Should a flip use the most expensive finishes available?
Not necessarily. Finishes should match or slightly exceed what comparable homes in the neighborhood offer. Going far beyond the street rarely pays back.

How important is natural light?
Very. Light, ceiling height and flow are among the first things buyers notice, and often matter more than individual finish selections.

Do design trends matter?
Buyers respond to current, durable design. Timeless materials and a clean palette usually age better than highly trend-driven choices.

title: Adding Square Footage: Where the Value Is in a Luxury Remodel
meta_description: Why adding square footage drives value in a Los Angeles luxury remodel, how floor-area rules limit it, and which additions buyers pay for most.
author: Oliver Thornton
body_html:
In Los Angeles, buyers pay for space, and the most reliable way to add value to an under-improved house is often to make it bigger. The best luxury remodel opportunities are homes that sit well below the size the lot allows, in neighborhoods where buyers will pay for more room.

Finding Unused Floor Area

Unused floor area is the gap between a home’s current size and the size its zoning allows. A 1,700-square-foot house on a lot that allows considerably more is a candidate; a house already built to the limit is not. Checking the floor-area rules, height limits, setbacks and any hillside rules before purchase tells you how much room there really is.

The Rules That Limit It

  • Floor-area limits. The City of Los Angeles caps residential floor area on single-family lots, with separate standards for hillside areas.
  • Height and setbacks. These shape where an addition can go.
  • Lot coverage and parking. Additions can trigger requirements that change the plan.
  • Overlays. Historic or design-review overlays add review and limit what can change; we generally avoid them.

What Buyers Pay For

AdditionWhy it adds value
Bedrooms and bathroomsMoves the home into a higher comparable set
A true primary suiteLarge bedroom, bath and closet are top priorities for luxury buyers
Open kitchen and family roomWhere buyers spend their time
Indoor-outdoor livingLarge openings to a usable yard or deck
Flexible spaceOffice, guest suite or media room

Don’t Outgrow the Street

Every neighborhood has a ceiling. Adding space past what comparable homes support rarely pays back, and in the City of Los Angeles a finished price above the Measure ULA threshold brings a transfer tax that can erase the gain. The goal is the right size for the street, not the biggest house on it.

Keeping It a Remodel

Adding space while keeping part of the existing structure can often keep a project in the remodel category for permitting and financing, which usually means less capital and a shorter schedule. See remodel vs. new construction.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does adding square footage always add value?
Not always. Space adds the most value when it creates rooms buyers want, such as bedrooms, bathrooms or a primary suite, and when the finished home still fits the neighborhood's price range.

What limits how much I can add in Los Angeles?
Zoning and floor-area rules. In the City of Los Angeles, single-family lots are subject to residential floor-area limits, with separate rules for hillside areas. Height, setbacks and lot coverage also apply.

What is unused floor area?
The difference between how large a home could be under the zoning rules and how large it is today. A house with significant unused floor area has room to grow.

Is a second story or a rear addition better?
It depends on the lot, the structure and neighborhood rules. A rear or side addition can be simpler structurally; a second story can add more space on a tight lot.

title: Do SB 684 Homes Need a DRE Public Report? The Fee-Simple Exemption Explained
meta_description: Why fee-simple SB 684 homes in a city usually don't need a California DRE public report, what Bus. & Prof. Code §11010.4 requires, and what breaks it.
author: Oliver Thornton
body_html:
One of the least discussed advantages of a fee-simple SB 684 project is what it can avoid: the California Department of Real Estate (DRE) public report. For many subdivisions, a public report is required before homes can be sold, and getting one adds an application, a review period, fees and months of time. Structured correctly, a fee-simple small-lot project in a city usually doesn’t need one.

What a Public Report Is

Under California’s Subdivided Lands Law, a subdivider generally has to file a notice of intention with the DRE and obtain a public report before selling lots in a subdivision. The report discloses information about the project to buyers. It is designed for consumer protection, and for condominiums and planned developments with shared ownership, it is an important one. For a handful of completed single-family homes on their own lots in a city, the law provides an exemption.

The Exemption: Bus. & Prof. Code §11010.4

Section 11010.4 says no notice of intention, and therefore no public report, is required for an offering of subdivided land that meets all of these conditions:

ConditionWhat it means for an SB 684 project
Inside a cityEach lot is located entirely within the boundaries of a city, not unincorporated county land
Completed homesEach lot is sold with a completed home and the improvements needed to occupy it, or with completion arrangements the city finds adequate
Not a common-interest projectThe project is a standard subdivision of separate lots, not a condominium, planned development, stock cooperative or similar structure
Blanket-encumbrance rulesThe subdivider complies with the law’s rules on blanket loans (such as a construction loan covering all the lots), so each buyer receives clear title to their lot

Why Fee-Simple SB 684 Projects Fit

A typical SB 684 project on the Westside checks every box. The lots are in a city such as Los Angeles, Culver City or Santa Monica. Each home sits on its own fee-simple lot with its own parcel number. There is no condominium map and no commonly owned building. And homes are sold one at a time as they are completed. That is why we sell completed homes rather than lots, and why the fee-simple path matters.

What Can Break the Exemption

  • Selling lots before homes are finished, without completion arrangements the city accepts
  • Common areas owned together, such as a jointly owned driveway or courtyard that turns the project into a planned development. Access is usually handled with easements instead; see shared driveways and maintenance agreements.
  • Choosing a condo or TIC structure, which brings the project back under the public report rules (see TIC vs. condo)
  • Unincorporated locations, which fall outside the city requirement
  • Loan structures that don’t let each lot be released from a blanket loan at closing

Why It Matters

Avoiding a public report removes a separate state approval from the critical path between finished homes and closings. Fewer months between completion and sale means less interest on the construction loan and a simpler sales process. It is one more reason fee-simple small-lot homes are a cleaner product than condominiums on the same site.

This is a general summary of California law, not legal advice. Whether a specific project qualifies depends on its facts and structure; confirm with real estate counsel and, where appropriate, the DRE.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is a DRE public report?
A disclosure document issued by the California Department of Real Estate for many subdivision sales. Obtaining one involves an application, review and fees, and it can add months to a project.

Do SB 684 homes need a DRE public report?
Often not. Under Business and Professions Code §11010.4, no DRE filing is required when each lot is in a city, is sold with a completed home, the project is not a condominium, planned development or similar common-interest project, and the law's blanket-encumbrance rules are met.

What would require a public report on an SB 684 project?
Selling lots before the homes are complete (without city-approved completion arrangements), structuring the project as a condominium or planned development with commonly owned areas, or a site outside city limits, among other things.

Do condos need a DRE public report?
Generally yes. Condominiums, planned developments and other common-interest developments are subdivisions that typically require a public report before units are sold.

title: Shared Driveways Without an HOA: Easements and Maintenance Agreements in SB 684 Projects
meta_description: How SB 684 small-lot homes share driveways and utilities without an HOA: access easements, maintenance agreements, and why the structure matters.
author: Oliver Thornton
body_html:
Six to ten homes on one former lot usually share something: a driveway, a walkway, a utility trench, a trash area. Buyers reasonably ask who owns those spaces and who pays to maintain them. In a fee-simple SB 684 project, the answer is usually easements and a maintenance agreement, not a traditional HOA.

Easements: Who Can Use What

An easement is a recorded right to use part of someone else’s property for a specific purpose. In a small-lot project, the shared driveway often runs across several lots, and recorded access easements give every owner the right to drive and walk over it. Utility easements do the same for sewer, water and power lines that cross lot lines.

Maintenance Agreements: Who Pays for What

A recorded maintenance agreement sets out how owners share the cost of keeping shared features in good shape. Typical provisions cover:

  • Which features are shared, such as the driveway, gates, lighting, trash enclosure and landscaping
  • How costs are split, often equally or by lot
  • How decisions are made and how repairs are scheduled
  • What happens if an owner doesn’t pay
  • Insurance and liability for shared areas

Why Not an HOA?

A homeowners association that owns common areas changes what the project is. Commonly owned areas can make a project a planned development, a type of common-interest development with its own rules, documents and, typically, a DRE public report requirement. Keeping each lot separately owned, with shared use handled by easements, is one of the conditions that lets fee-simple homes in a city avoid a public report; see do SB 684 homes need a DRE public report?

What Buyers Should Review

  • The recorded easements, and which lots they burden and benefit
  • The maintenance agreement and any expected annual costs
  • Parking assignments and guest access
  • Rules for trash pickup, deliveries and gates

For a buyer, the result is simple: you own your home and the land under it, share a few features with neighbors on clear written terms, and avoid the monthly dues and shared-building decisions that come with a condominium.

General information, not legal advice. Each project’s easements and agreements depend on its site plan and local requirements.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do SB 684 homes have an HOA?
Usually not in the condominium sense. Fee-simple small-lot homes typically share access and utilities through recorded easements and a maintenance agreement rather than a homeowners association that owns common property.

Who owns the shared driveway in an SB 684 project?
Often the driveway sits on the individual lots, with recorded easements giving each owner the right to use it. The exact approach depends on the site plan and local requirements.

How are shared costs split?
A recorded maintenance agreement typically sets out how owners share the cost of maintaining shared driveways, utilities, trash areas and landscaping.

Why not just create an HOA?
A commonly owned area can turn the project into a planned development, which brings additional rules and can require a DRE public report.

title: Can Buyers Get a Conventional Mortgage on an SB 684 Home?
meta_description: Why fee-simple SB 684 homes usually qualify for conventional mortgages like any single-family house, and how that compares with condos and TICs.
author: Oliver Thornton
body_html:
The most important feature of a fee-simple SB 684 home may be one buyers never see: it can be financed like an ordinary house. That single fact shapes who can buy these homes, how fast they sell, and what they sell for.

Why Fee Simple Finances Like a House

Each SB 684 home sits on its own legal lot, with its own assessor’s parcel number, owned outright by the buyer. To a lender, that looks like a single-family home: there is no shared building, no condominium project to review, and no fractional ownership. Buyers can generally use the same conventional mortgages, and often the same first-time-buyer programs, they would use for any other house.

How It Compares

Fee-simple small-lot homeCondominiumTenancy in common
What you ownThe home and the land under itA unit plus a share of common areasA fractional share of the whole property
Typical loanStandard single-family mortgageCondo mortgage, subject to project reviewSpecialized fractional TIC loan
Project-level reviewGenerally noneOften requiredLender-specific
Buyer poolBroadestBroadNarrowest

Why This Matters for Sellers and Investors

A deeper buyer pool supports pricing and shortens time on market, which in turn shortens the time a construction loan is outstanding. It is a big part of why fee-simple subdivision is generally a stronger exit than a condo or TIC on the same site, and why we choose it wherever a site qualifies. See also how fee-simple small-lot homes are priced.

What Buyers Should Still Check

  • That the final map has recorded and the home has its own parcel number
  • Any shared-driveway easements and maintenance agreement
  • The appraisal, which will rely on comparable sales of similar new homes
  • Program-specific property requirements if using FHA, VA or other programs

General information, not lending advice. Loan availability and terms depend on the borrower, the property and the lender.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I use a conventional mortgage to buy an SB 684 home?
Usually yes. A fee-simple SB 684 home sits on its own legal lot with its own parcel number, so lenders generally underwrite it like any other single-family home.

Is financing different from buying a condo?
Condo loans can depend on the lender's review of the whole condominium project, including its budget and owner-occupancy. A fee-simple home generally doesn't require that project-level review.

Can first-time buyers use FHA or other programs on SB 684 homes?
Often, subject to the program's normal property and borrower requirements. Buyers should confirm eligibility with their lender.

Why does financing matter so much for small-lot homes?
The easier a home is to finance, the more buyers can purchase it, which supports both price and speed of sale.

title: What Is California’s Starter Home Revitalization Act?
meta_description: California's Starter Home Revitalization Act explained: why it was passed, how SB 684, SB 1123 and AB 130 built it, and what it means for new starter homes.
author: Oliver Thornton
body_html:
The Starter Home Revitalization Act (SHRA) is the name of the California framework that most people know by its bill numbers: SB 684 and SB 1123. Its goal is in the name: make it easier to build small, for-sale starter homes on infill land, so more Californians can own instead of rent.

The Problem It Addresses

For decades, the missing piece of California housing has been the modest for-sale home. Single-family zoning limited most land to one house, and subdividing a lot into several homes usually meant discretionary hearings, environmental review and years of uncertainty. The few small-lot homes that got built carried the cost of that process. The Act targets that bottleneck directly.

How the Act Was Built

BillWhat it did
SB 684Created a ministerial path to subdivide qualifying multifamily-zoned lots into up to 10 lots and 10 homes
SB 1123 (effective July 1, 2025)Extended the path to vacant single-family lots, refined standards and added tenancy in common as an ownership option
AB 130 (effective July 1, 2025)Further amended the Act

What It Allows

  • Up to 10 lots and 10 homes on a qualifying site
  • Ministerial approval, with no public hearing and no CEQA review, and a decision within 60 days of a complete application
  • State-set limits on setbacks, lot size and floor area that make compact site plans possible
  • Homes averaging no more than 1,750 net habitable square feet, keeping the product at starter-home scale

What It Protects

The Act screens out sites with environmental hazards, such as high fire hazard severity zones and flood zones, and sites where building would displace renters or protected housing. Those screens are why most qualifying land sits in the flats of established neighborhoods. See tenant history rules.

What It Means in Practice

On the Westside, the Act has turned older homes on multifamily-zoned lots into sites for six to nine new fee-simple homes, each on its own lot and each financeable with a conventional mortgage. Early projects in Culver City and Santa Monica show how quickly the pathway is maturing. For the full rules, see our SB 684 and SB 1123 guide.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Starter Home Revitalization Act?
A California law, created by SB 684, that lets qualifying lots be subdivided into up to 10 small fee-simple lots with homes, approved ministerially without a public hearing or CEQA review.

Which bills make up the Starter Home Revitalization Act?
SB 684 created it, SB 1123 extended it to vacant single-family lots effective July 1, 2025, and AB 130 also amended it effective July 1, 2025.

Why was the Starter Home Revitalization Act passed?
To increase homeownership by making it easier to build small, lower-cost for-sale homes on infill land.

Is the Starter Home Revitalization Act the same as SB 9?
No. SB 9 is a separate law allowing up to four units through a lot split on single-family lots. The Starter Home Revitalization Act allows up to ten homes on qualifying sites.

title: SB 684 and Property Taxes: How New Small-Lot Homes Are Assessed
meta_description: How property taxes work on SB 684 projects: Prop 13 base values, separate parcel numbers, new-construction assessments and supplemental bills for buyers.
author: Oliver Thornton
body_html:
Property taxes on an SB 684 project change as the project moves from one lot to several homes. Owners selling land, developers underwriting a project and buyers of the finished homes all run into the same few rules. Here is how they work in general terms.

The Basics: Proposition 13

In California, a property’s assessed value is generally set when it changes ownership and when new construction is completed, and then rises only modestly each year. The annual tax is a percentage of that assessed value plus local assessments. Those two triggers, a sale and new construction, drive almost everything on an SB 684 project.

How Taxes Change Through a Project

StageWhat usually happens
Developer buys the lotThe purchase price sets a new base value for the single parcel
Final map recordsThe county creates new parcels and allocates value among them; each gets its own parcel number and bill
Homes are completedThe value of the new construction is added to each parcel’s assessed value
Each home sellsThe buyer’s purchase price generally sets that home’s new base value

Supplemental Tax Bills

When a property changes hands or new construction is completed partway through the tax year, the county issues a supplemental bill for the difference between the old and new values for the rest of that year. Buyers of new SB 684 homes should expect one after closing, and lenders and escrow officers usually flag it. It often arrives months later, so it is worth budgeting for.

What Each Party Should Know

  • Owners selling a lot: the sale ends your Prop 13 base on that property; ask your tax advisor how it fits your situation.
  • Developers: carry costs include property taxes on the land during entitlement and construction, rising as homes are completed.
  • Buyers: budget for both the regular annual bill and a supplemental bill based on your purchase price.

Transfer Taxes Are Separate

Property tax is different from the transfer taxes charged at sale. Those vary by city: the City of Los Angeles has Measure ULA on higher-value sales, and neighboring cities have their own rules. Entry-level fee-simple homes generally sell below the steepest transfer-tax thresholds.

General information, not tax advice. Assessments and bills are set by the county assessor and tax collector; consult a tax professional about your situation.

Frequently Asked Questions

How are SB 684 homes taxed?
Each home, once on its own parcel, is taxed separately. Under Proposition 13, the base value generally resets on a change of ownership and new construction is added to the assessed value when completed.

What is a supplemental tax bill?
A separate bill issued after a change of ownership or completed new construction, covering the difference between the old and new assessed values for the rest of the tax year.

Do buyers of new SB 684 homes pay supplemental taxes?
Typically yes. Buyers of newly built homes should expect a supplemental bill after closing, in addition to the regular annual bill.

When do the new lots get their own tax bills?
After the final map records and the county assessor assigns new parcel numbers, which can take some time.

title: SB 684 vs. Los Angeles’ Small Lot Subdivision Ordinance
meta_description: How California's SB 684 compares to Los Angeles' Small Lot Subdivision Ordinance: approval path, unit caps, design rules, timelines and when each makes sense.
author: Oliver Thornton
body_html:
Los Angeles was building fee-simple small-lot homes long before SB 684. The city’s Small Lot Subdivision Ordinance, in use since 2005, let developers split multifamily and some commercial lots into small parcels with a house on each, and it produced many of the narrow townhome-style homes seen across Silver Lake, Echo Park and the Westside. SB 684 created a second, state-level path. Here is how they compare.

The Core Difference: Discretion

The city’s small lot process typically involves discretionary review: a decision-maker applies judgment, design guidelines apply, and neighbors can weigh in or appeal. SB 684 is ministerial: if a qualifying project meets objective standards, the city must approve it, with no hearing and no CEQA review, and a decision is due within 60 days of a complete application. For a small builder, that difference turns entitlement from an open question into a schedule.

Side by Side

SB 684 / SB 1123LA Small Lot Subdivision
SourceState lawCity of Los Angeles ordinance
ApprovalMinisterial; no hearing, no CEQATypically discretionary review
Size cap10 lots and 10 homesNo 10-home cap; set by zoning and density
Home sizeAverage no more than 1,750 net habitable sq ftSet by zoning and design standards
SetbacksSide and rear capped at 4 ft from the original lot linePer city small lot standards
Site screensFire, flood, fault, habitat, tenant-history and other exclusionsPer city code and CEQA review
ProductFee-simple homes on individual lotsFee-simple homes on individual lots

When the City Path Still Makes Sense

  • Larger sites that can carry more than ten homes
  • Commercial or mixed zones where the city ordinance applies but SB 684 may not
  • Sites that fail an SB 684 screen, such as certain tenant-history or hazard exclusions, but can still be entitled through discretionary review

When SB 684 Wins

On a qualifying multifamily-zoned lot of roughly 5,000 to 10,000 square feet, where six to ten homes fit, SB 684’s ministerial approval, fixed review clock and state-set setback and floor-area floors usually make it the stronger path. It removes the hearing risk that can stall a small project for months and makes the timeline easier to finance.

What Stays the Same

Whichever path a project takes, the buyer experience is similar: a new home on its own lot, with its own parcel number, financeable with a conventional mortgage. That is the advantage of fee-simple small-lot housing over condominiums, and it is why both paths exist. For how either path moves from application to permits, see the Los Angeles entitlement process, step by step.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does Los Angeles still allow small lot subdivisions under its own ordinance?
Yes. The City of Los Angeles Small Lot Subdivision Ordinance, in use since 2005 and updated since, remains available on eligible sites. SB 684 adds a separate, state-level ministerial path.

Which is faster, SB 684 or the LA Small Lot Ordinance?
SB 684 is generally faster because qualifying projects are approved ministerially, with a 60-day decision on a complete application. City small lot projects typically involve discretionary review.

Can a small lot project exceed 10 homes?
Under SB 684, no: the cap is 10 lots and 10 homes. Larger projects generally have to use another path, such as the city's small lot rules or a conventional subdivision.

Do both create fee-simple homes?
Yes. Both paths are designed to create individual fee-simple lots that each carry a home, rather than condominium units.

title: How to Spot an SB 684 Lot: A Checklist for Agents and Owners
meta_description: A practical checklist for spotting SB 684 lots: zoning, lot size, fire zones, tenant history and how to check them with ZIMAS and city maps in minutes.
author: Oliver Thornton
body_html:
Most SB 684 sites don’t look like development sites. They look like an older house on a slightly larger-than-average lot on a multifamily-zoned block. If you know what to check, you can screen a listing in a few minutes. This checklist is for listing agents, buyer’s agents, wholesalers and owners.

The Five-Minute Screen

CheckWhat you want to seeWhere to look
ZoningMultifamily zoning (or a vacant single-family lot)ZIMAS (City of LA) or the city’s zoning map
Lot size5,000 sq ft or more; 6,000+ is betterZIMAS, county assessor, MLS
Fire zoneNot in a high or very high fire hazard severity zoneZIMAS hazards tab or the state fire hazard map
LocationIn the flats, with urban uses on most sidesAny map
OccupancyOwner-occupied or no tenants in the last five yearsThe owner; city rent and Ellis records
Prior splitsNot already split under SB 9 or SB 684Recorded maps; the city

Using ZIMAS (City of Los Angeles)

For addresses inside the City of Los Angeles, ZIMAS is the fastest first check. Search the address, then look at the zoning designation, the lot area, and the hazards information, including whether the parcel sits in a very high fire hazard severity zone. Remember that many addresses with a “Los Angeles” mailing address are actually in Culver City, Santa Monica or unincorporated county, which have their own maps and rules.

Signals That a Listing Is Worth a Closer Look

  • An older single-family home on a lot zoned for two or more units
  • A wide lot, a corner lot, or a lot that runs street to alley
  • A long-time owner-occupant, an estate or a trust sale
  • A flat lot in a neighborhood where new townhomes already sell well
  • Days on market piling up because buyers are valuing only the house

Red Flags

  • Current tenants, or a recent Ellis Act withdrawal (see tenant history rules)
  • A hillside or fire-zone location
  • Historic overlays, coastal-zone permits or a lot already split
  • A lot too small or too narrow for six homes with parking

Found One?

If a property clears most of this list, it is worth sending over. We reply within two business days with a yes, a no, or our questions, and we honor agent commissions. Submit a property, or read what owners should know before selling.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is ZIMAS?
ZIMAS is the City of Los Angeles' free online zoning and parcel map. It shows a parcel's zoning, lot size and many overlays, including fire hazard severity zones, for properties inside the City of Los Angeles.

What zoning should I look for?
Multifamily zoning is the clearest SB 684 path. In the City of Los Angeles that includes zones such as RD, R2 and R3; other cities use their own zone names, so check the local zoning map.

Is a single-family lot ever an SB 684 site?
A vacant single-family-zoned lot can qualify under SB 1123. A single-family lot with an occupied house on it generally does not.

Can I check tenant history online?
Partly. Cities with rent registries or Ellis Act records may show some history, but the owner is usually the best source. A developer confirms it in due diligence.

title: SB 684 Site Planning: How Six to Ten Homes Fit on One Lot
meta_description: How SB 684 site plans work: lot layouts, 4-foot setbacks, parking, driveways, floor-area floors and rooftop decks that fit six to ten homes on one lot.
author: Oliver Thornton
body_html:
The question every owner and agent asks about an SB 684 site is the same: how many homes fit? The answer comes from the site plan, and SB 684 gives designers more room than most people expect.

The Rules That Make It Possible

StandardWhat SB 684 allows
Lots and homesUp to 10 of each
Minimum new lot600 sq ft (multifamily) / 1,200 sq ft (vacant single-family)
Side and rear setbacksNo more than 4 ft from the original lot line
Space between homesNot required beyond building-code minimums
Lot width, depth, frontageNo local minimums
Floor areaCity can’t set FAR below 1.0 (3–7 homes) or 1.25 (8–10)
Home sizeAverage of no more than 1,750 net habitable sq ft
ParkingNo more than 1 space per home; none near qualifying transit

Common Layouts

  • Shared drive down one side. Homes line up along a single driveway, each with a garage or carport space. Works on deeper lots.
  • Street-to-alley. Homes face the street and the alley, with parking taken from the alley. This is one reason alley lots are so valuable.
  • Corner lots. Two frontages mean homes can face two streets, with simpler access and more light.
  • Front and rear clusters. Homes grouped at the front and back of the lot around a shared access path.

What Makes Small Homes Feel Large

With footprints this tight, design does the work. Three-story plans put living space up and parking down. Rooftop decks add private outdoor space in neighborhoods where yards are rare. Large windows on the long side of each home, and careful placement so homes don’t look straight into each other, make 1,100 to 1,600 square feet feel generous. At 1949 17th Street in Santa Monica, for example, nine homes of about 1,150 to 1,600 square feet each have a private rooftop deck.

Practical Constraints

  • Fire access. Fire department access and hydrant distance often shape the plan more than zoning does.
  • Utilities. Each home needs its own connections, so sewer and water capacity matter.
  • Trees and grades. Protected trees and slope reduce usable area.
  • Trash and mail. Small details that still need a spot on the plan.

Lot Shape Matters as Much as Size

A 6,000-square-foot lot that is wide or runs street to alley can outperform a deeper, narrower lot of the same size. That is why corner and alley lots are at the top of our SB 684 buy box, and why we look at shape before we look at price.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many homes fit on a 6,000 square foot lot under SB 684?
It depends on width, access and the city's standards, but a well-shaped 6,000 square foot lot can often carry around six fee-simple homes with one parking space each.

What setbacks apply under SB 684?
Side and rear setbacks are capped at 4 feet from the original lot line, and no separation is required between homes beyond building-code minimums.

Does SB 684 require parking?
A city cannot require more than one space per home, and cannot require parking near qualifying transit.

How big can SB 684 homes be?
The average home cannot exceed 1,750 net habitable square feet, and the city cannot set a floor-area ratio below 1.0 for three to seven homes or 1.25 for eight to ten.

title: SB 684 on the Westside: Mar Vista, Palms, Del Rey, West LA and Westchester
meta_description: Where SB 684 small-lot homes fit on the Westside: Mar Vista, Palms, Del Rey, West LA and Westchester, and what owners in each neighborhood should know.
author: Oliver Thornton
body_html:
The Westside is where SB 684 fits best in Los Angeles: flat land, blocks zoned for more than one home, older houses on generous lots, and buyers who want a new house close to the beach and the job centers of Culver City, Playa Vista and Santa Monica. This guide looks at the City of Los Angeles neighborhoods where we see the most potential.

Mar Vista

Mar Vista mixes single-family streets with multifamily-zoned blocks, many still holding mid-century homes on lots of 5,000 to 7,000 square feet. Strong schools and a loyal owner-occupant base make it a natural market for new fee-simple homes. The best sites are on multifamily-zoned blocks near Venice Boulevard and the neighborhood’s commercial corridors.

Palms

Palms is one of the denser parts of the Westside, with many multifamily-zoned lots and quick access to the Expo Line and Culver City. Tenant history is the main hurdle: much of Palms is rental housing, so owner-occupied or long-vacant homes are the sites that qualify.

Del Rey

Del Rey sits between Mar Vista, Culver City and Playa Vista, with flat land and a mix of zoning. Its location near Silicon Beach employers supports demand for new two- and three-bedroom homes.

West Los Angeles

West LA, around Sawtelle and the 405, has many multifamily-zoned lots and some of the strongest demand on the Westside. Lot sizes vary widely, so site shape and access often decide whether six homes fit.

Westchester

Westchester offers larger lots and flat terrain near LAX-area and Playa Vista employment. It is mostly single-family zoning, so the strongest SB 684 candidates are its multifamily-zoned pockets, or vacant single-family lots under SB 1123.

What Applies Across All Five

  • These are City of Los Angeles neighborhoods, so check zoning and hazards in ZIMAS; see how to spot an SB 684 lot.
  • Tenant history and the city’s rent rules are the most common disqualifiers.
  • Most of the Westside flats sit outside fire hazard severity zones, which is part of why the area works.
  • Entry-level fee-simple homes sell well below the Measure ULA threshold.

Next door, Culver City and Santa Monica have their own rules and their own early SB 684 approvals.

Frequently Asked Questions

Are Mar Vista, Palms and Del Rey in the City of Los Angeles?
Yes. They are neighborhoods within the City of Los Angeles, so City of Los Angeles zoning, ZIMAS and Measure ULA apply. Culver City and Santa Monica are separate cities.

Why are Westside neighborhoods good for SB 684?
They combine flat land, multifamily-zoned blocks with older homes, strong owner-occupant demand, and job centers nearby, which supports new fee-simple starter homes.

Does Measure ULA affect SB 684 homes on the Westside?
Rarely. Entry-level fee-simple homes generally sell well below the Measure ULA threshold, so the tax is usually not a factor for individual small-lot home sales.

Do you buy outside these neighborhoods?
Selectively. We also consider Culver City, Santa Monica, Venice, Brentwood and select coastal markets where new homes have strong per-square-foot resale.

title: Sell or Develop? An Owner’s Guide to SB 684 Options
meta_description: Own a lot that might qualify for SB 684? Compare selling to a developer with building yourself: time, capital, risk, financing and what each path involves.
author: Oliver Thornton
body_html:
If your lot might qualify under SB 684, you have a real choice: sell the land to a small-lot developer, or take on the project yourself. Both can make sense. This guide lays out what each path involves so you can decide with clear eyes.

The Two Paths

Sell to a developerDevelop it yourself
TimelineWeeks to a few months to closeRoughly two years or more to finished homes, then sales
CapitalNoneDesign, permits, carry and the equity lenders require
FinancingNoneAcquisition or construction loans, usually with personal guarantees
RiskLow once in escrowEntitlement, cost, schedule and sale-price risk
WorkMinimalManaging architects, engineers, contractors and sales
UpsideA price that reflects the lot’s development valueAny profit the project produces, if it goes to plan

What Developing Really Involves

  • Entitlement. A site plan, subdivision application, map approval and plan check, typically about 12 months to ready-to-issue permits.
  • Financing. A construction loan sized against the entitled and as-complete values, usually with personal guarantees. See how SB 684 financing works.
  • Construction. About 12 months for six to ten homes, with contingency for the unexpected.
  • The final map and sales. Recording the map, then selling each home individually. See what happens at a final map.

Questions to Ask Yourself

  • Do I want a defined price now, or a larger but uncertain outcome in two to three years?
  • Can I carry the project if costs rise or sales slow?
  • Am I willing to personally guarantee construction debt?
  • Do I have, or can I hire, a team that has done this before?

Why Many Owners Sell

For most owners, especially long-time residents, estates and trusts, selling to an experienced small-lot developer captures much of the land’s new value without the time, debt and risk of building. The key is making sure the price reflects what the lot can become, not just the house on it. Our guide to selling your lot to an SB 684 developer explains how that pricing works.

This article is general information, not legal, tax or financial advice. Talk with your own advisors before deciding.

Frequently Asked Questions

Should I develop my lot myself under SB 684?
Only if you are prepared for the time, capital and risk: roughly two years from entitlement through construction, construction financing that usually requires guarantees, and the work of selling homes one by one.

How long does an SB 684 project take?
On recent projects, about 12 months from the start of entitlement to ready-to-issue permits, trending toward 9 to 10 months, then about 12 months of construction, followed by sales.

What do I need to develop it myself?
An architect and civil engineer, a general contractor, construction financing, and the capital to carry the project until the homes sell.

Is selling to a developer simpler?
Usually. You get a defined price and closing date, and the developer takes on entitlement, construction and sales risk.

title: SB 684 in Santa Monica: Small-Lot Homes in a Supply-Constrained City
meta_description: How SB 684 works in Santa Monica: which lots qualify, rent control and tenant history, timelines, and a nine-home approval on 17th Street.
author: Oliver Thornton
body_html:
Few cities in Southern California need new starter homes more than Santa Monica, and few have been harder to build in. California’s SB 684 changes that for a specific kind of site: a multifamily-zoned lot in the flats that can be subdivided into several small fee-simple homes, approved ministerially with no public hearing.

Why Santa Monica Is Different

Santa Monica combines strong demand, limited new supply and a large share of rent-controlled housing. That last point matters most for SB 684: the law protects existing renters, and Santa Monica’s rent-control history means tenant history can disqualify many otherwise attractive lots. The sites that work are typically owner-occupied homes, or properties that have not been rented in years, on multifamily-zoned land.

A Recent Example: 1949 17th Street

At 1949 17th Street, a principal-owned project developed through Thornton Development Group, the city approved nine fee-simple homes on one subdivided lot under SB 684. It was only the second SB 684 approval in Santa Monica, and it took about eight months from the start of entitlement to City approval. The property had not been used as rental housing in more than 30 years, which kept it clear of the rent-control issues that stop many sites. Eight of the planned homes are about 1,150 square feet and one is about 1,600, each on its own parcel with its own rooftop deck. The project is now near ready-to-issue permits, with construction expected to start in November 2026 (estimated).

What Makes a Santa Monica Lot Work

  • Zoning. Multifamily zoning gives the clearest path; single-family lots qualify under SB 1123 only if vacant.
  • Tenant history. Owner-occupied, or no rental history in the last five years, and no Ellis Act withdrawal in the last fifteen. See Ellis Act and tenant history.
  • Size. Enough land for at least six homes; most strong sites are 6,000 square feet or more.
  • Hazards. Outside fire hazard severity zones and the law’s other exclusions.
  • Coastal review. Sites that need Coastal Commission review add time and uncertainty; we generally pass on them.

Taxes on Sale

Santa Monica is outside the City of Los Angeles, so Measure ULA does not apply. The city has its own transfer tax on higher-value sales, which sellers should factor into pricing. Entry-level fee-simple homes generally sell well below the price points where the steepest transfer taxes apply.

Thinking About Selling?

If you own a multifamily-zoned lot in Santa Monica with an older home on it, the land may be worth more to a small-lot developer than the house is to a typical buyer. Read selling your lot to an SB 684 developer, or send us the address for a quick read.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does SB 684 apply in Santa Monica?
Yes. SB 684 is state law and applies in Santa Monica to qualifying multifamily-zoned lots, with SB 1123 extending it to qualifying vacant single-family lots. The city processes applications under its own procedures.

How does Santa Monica rent control affect SB 684 sites?
Tenant history is one of the first screens. Sites with recent tenants or rent-controlled units can be disqualified or face additional requirements, so owner-occupied homes, or properties with no rental history, are the strongest candidates.

How long does SB 684 approval take in Santa Monica?
On 1949 17th Street, a principal-owned project, it took about eight months from the start of entitlement to City approval. Every site differs.

Does Measure ULA apply in Santa Monica?
No. Measure ULA applies only within City of Los Angeles limits. Santa Monica has its own transfer tax on higher-value sales.

title: SB 684 in Culver City: Inside the City’s First Small-Lot Approvals
meta_description: SB 684 in Culver City: the first approval in the city, what qualifies, timelines to ready-to-issue permits, and what owners of multifamily lots should know.
author: Oliver Thornton
body_html:
Culver City has become one of the most active places in Los Angeles County for SB 684 small-lot homes. Its multifamily-zoned blocks, strong owner-occupant demand and location between the Westside and downtown make it close to ideal for new fee-simple starter homes. This guide covers what has happened so far and what owners should know.

The First Approval in the City

The Culver VI at 3850 Westwood Boulevard was the first SB 684 approval in Culver City. It subdivides one lot into six developable fee-simple lots, and its tentative tract map has been approved. When the project refinanced into its construction loan, the lots appraised as entitled land well above the purchase price, and the loan closed with no cash required at closing. The project is about three months from ready-to-issue building permits, with construction expected to start in January 2027 (estimated).

More Projects in the Pipeline

ProjectHomesStatus
The Culver VI, 3850 Westwood6Map approved; nearing ready-to-issue permits
The Harter V, 4058 Harter5In entitlement
The Helms VI, 3562 Helms6In entitlement
The Sentney VI, 3011 Sentney6 (about 1,300 sq ft each)In escrow

These are Assemble Capital projects developed by Thornton Development Group. Timelines are estimates and plans may change.

What Qualifies in Culver City

  • Multifamily zoning is the most direct path. Many Culver City blocks zoned for two or more units have a single older house on a lot that can now carry six homes.
  • Lot size of at least 5,000 square feet, ideally 6,000 or more.
  • Tenant history: owner-occupied, or no rental history in the last five years, and no Ellis Act withdrawal in the last fifteen. Culver City has its own rent-control rules, so tenant history is checked early.
  • Hazards: outside fire hazard severity zones and the law’s other exclusions, which favors the flats.

Timelines We Have Seen

Across our Culver City projects, the path from the start of entitlement to ready-to-issue permits has taken about 12 months, and it is trending toward 9–10 months as the building department gets familiar with the law. Construction then takes about 12 months. See the entitlement process, step by step.

Taxes on Sale

Culver City is a separate city from Los Angeles, so Measure ULA does not apply. The city has its own transfer tax on higher-value sales. Entry-level fee-simple homes sell at price points where that tax is far less of a factor than on luxury sales.

Own a Lot in Culver City?

If you own a multifamily-zoned lot with an older home on it, it may be worth a quick look. Read what to expect when you sell to an SB 684 developer, or send us the address.

Frequently Asked Questions

Has Culver City approved SB 684 projects?
Yes. The Culver VI at 3850 Westwood Boulevard, an Assemble Capital project, was the first SB 684 approval in Culver City, and several more projects are moving through the process.

Which Culver City lots qualify for SB 684?
Generally multifamily-zoned lots in the flats that clear the law's tenant-history and hazard screens. Vacant single-family lots can qualify under SB 1123.

How long does an SB 684 project take in Culver City?
On recent projects, about 12 months from the start of entitlement to ready-to-issue permits, trending toward 9 to 10 months, then about 12 months of construction. These are estimates.

Does Measure ULA apply in Culver City?
No. Culver City is a separate city from Los Angeles, so Measure ULA does not apply. Culver City has its own transfer tax on higher-value sales.

title: How Fee-Simple Small-Lot Homes Are Priced
meta_description: What drives the price of new fee-simple small-lot homes in Los Angeles: comparable sales, size, parking, outdoor space and why fee simple beats a condo.
author: Oliver Thornton
body_html:
An SB 684 project lives or dies on what its finished homes sell for. Every number upstream, from the land price to the construction loan, rests on that estimate. Here is how new fee-simple small-lot homes are typically priced, and what moves the price up or down.

Start With the Comparable Sales

Appraisers and buyers anchor on recent sales of similar homes nearby: size, bedroom count, age, condition and location. For a new small-lot home, the most useful comparables are other new or recently built townhomes and small-lot homes, and newer condos, adjusted for the advantages of owning the land. Price per square foot is the common shorthand, but it is a starting point, not an answer.

What Moves the Price

FactorWhy it matters
Fee-simple titleBuyer owns the land and can use a conventional mortgage; no condo HOA
NeighborhoodSchools, walkability and the surrounding price level set the ceiling
Size and layoutTwo- and three-bedroom plans with usable living space sell to the widest pool
ParkingA dedicated space is a major selling point on the Westside
Outdoor spaceRooftop decks and private yards add real value in dense neighborhoods
Finish levelQuality finishes support pricing; over-building rarely pays back
Position on the siteStreet-facing and corner homes often price differently from interior ones

Fee Simple vs. Condo vs. TIC

The same building sold three ways would price three ways. A fee-simple home on its own parcel generally sells at a premium to a comparable condo, and a condo generally sells above a comparable tenancy-in-common unit, mostly because of financing: the easier it is for a buyer to get a conventional mortgage, the deeper the buyer pool. That is why, where a site qualifies, we choose the fee-simple path.

Selling Home by Home

Small-lot homes are usually sold one at a time as they are completed, which lets pricing respond to the market as the project sells. The construction loan is typically repaid home by home, with each closing releasing a lot. See how SB 684 construction financing works.

The Honest Caveat

Projected prices are estimates. Markets move between acquisition and sale, and a project that pencils at today’s prices can be tested by a slower market. Disciplined underwriting tests the plan against lower prices and longer sale periods, not just the base case.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why do fee-simple homes sell for more than comparable condos?
Buyers own the land under the home, can use conventional financing, and usually avoid HOA dues and shared-building decisions. Those advantages tend to support a premium over condos of similar size.

What size are SB 684 homes?
The law caps the average at 1,750 net habitable square feet. Many Westside projects build two- and three-bedroom homes of roughly 1,100 to 1,600 square feet.

Who buys small-lot homes?
Mostly owner-occupants: first-time buyers, couples and small families who want a new house rather than a condo, in a neighborhood they might otherwise be priced out of.

Are small-lot home prices guaranteed?
No. Prices depend on the market at the time of sale, and finished homes can sell for less or take longer to sell than projected.

title: Ellis Act and Tenant History: What Can Disqualify an SB 684 Site
meta_description: The tenant-history and Ellis Act rules that can disqualify an SB 684 site, what counts, how to check, and which properties make the strongest candidates.
author: Oliver Thornton
body_html:
The fastest way for an otherwise perfect lot to fail an SB 684 screen is its tenant history. California’s small-lot laws were written to add housing without displacing renters, so they exclude sites with recent tenants, protected units or a recent Ellis Act withdrawal. This guide explains what developers check and why.

What the Screens Look For

ScreenWhat it means in practice
Recent tenant occupancyHousing occupied by tenants within roughly the last five years can disqualify a site
Ellis Act withdrawalUnits withdrawn from the rental market under the Ellis Act within the last 15 years generally disqualify a site
Rent-controlled or affordable unitsUnits subject to rent control or affordability covenants generally cannot be demolished under the Act

This is a screening summary, not legal advice. The exact language and local implementation vary, so confirm a specific site with the city and qualified counsel.

What the Ellis Act Is

The Ellis Act lets an owner leave the rental business by withdrawing every unit in a building from the rental market, following local notice and relocation rules. Cities such as Los Angeles and Santa Monica keep records of these withdrawals. Because a withdrawal is a public event, it is one of the easiest things for a developer to find, and one of the hardest problems to fix.

The Strongest Candidates

  • Owner-occupied homes, especially long-held family homes
  • Properties with no rental history in the last five years
  • Vacant lots, which also open the SB 1123 path in single-family zones

A single-family home that was rented a decade ago and has been owner-occupied since may still work. A duplex with tenants today usually won’t.

What to Gather Before You Call

  • Who has lived in the property over the last five years, and when
  • Any leases, rent-registry filings or relocation payments
  • Whether any units were ever withdrawn under the Ellis Act
  • Whether any unit is subject to rent control or an affordability covenant

Having that history ready is the fastest way to a real answer. If the tenant history is clean and the lot is large enough for six or more homes, send it to us.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Ellis Act?
A California law that lets an owner exit the rental business by withdrawing all units in a building from the rental market, subject to local procedures, notice periods and tenant relocation requirements.

How does an Ellis Act withdrawal affect SB 684 eligibility?
A site where rental units were withdrawn under the Ellis Act within the past 15 years generally cannot use SB 684.

Does any past rental disqualify a site?
Not necessarily. The key screens look at tenant occupancy in the recent past, generally the last five years, and at rent-controlled or affordable units. Owner-occupied homes and properties with no recent rental history are the strongest candidates.

How can I check a property's history?
Start with the owner's records and the city's rent-registry or Ellis Act records where they exist. A developer will confirm with the city during due diligence.

title: What Happens at a Final Map: The Last Step Before Selling Small-Lot Homes
meta_description: Tentative vs. final map explained: what a final map is, when it records, how new parcel numbers are created, and why individual homes can't sell until it does.
author: Oliver Thornton
body_html:
