Approval of an SB 684 subdivision is a milestone, not the finish line. The approval creates a tentative map. The lots don’t legally exist until a final map records, and individual homes generally can’t be sold until they do. Here is what happens in between.

Tentative Map vs. Final Map

Tentative mapFinal map
What it isThe approved subdivision plan, with conditionsThe recorded, surveyed map that legally creates the lots
Who actsPlanning approvesSurveyor prepares; city engineer checks; county records
ResultPermission to proceedNew legal parcels, then new parcel numbers

What Happens Between the Two

  • Satisfying conditions. The tentative approval comes with conditions, such as utility connections, easements, fees or street improvements.
  • Survey and map preparation. A licensed surveyor prepares the final map to the city’s technical standards.
  • Map check. The city engineer or surveyor reviews it, often through a round or two of corrections.
  • Guarantees. Where improvements aren’t finished, the city may require an agreement or bond to secure them.
  • Recording. Once approved, the map records with the county, and the lots legally exist.

New Parcel Numbers

After recording, the county assessor assigns each new lot its own assessor’s parcel number. That step can take weeks to months. It matters because a separate APN is what lets each home be taxed, financed and sold on its own, which is the core advantage of a fee-simple small-lot subdivision. See how fee-simple small-lot homes are priced.

Why Timing Matters

The final map is often on the critical path to sales. If it records late, finished homes can sit waiting while interest accrues on the construction loan. Experienced developers work the final map in parallel with construction, so the lots exist by the time the homes are ready. Where the map falls in the schedule depends on the city’s conditions; see the Los Angeles entitlement process, step by step.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the difference between a tentative map and a final map?
A tentative map is the approved plan for a subdivision, with conditions. A final map is the recorded, surveyed document that legally creates the new lots once those conditions are met.

When can individual small-lot homes be sold?
Generally only after the final map records and the new lots legally exist, so each home can be conveyed on its own parcel.

Who assigns the new parcel numbers?
The county assessor assigns new assessor's parcel numbers (APNs) after the final map records, which can take some time.

Can construction start before the final map records?
It depends on the jurisdiction and project. Some projects build under permits issued before the final map records; others record first. Timing is set by the city's conditions.

title: Hillside Development Costs in Los Angeles: What Makes a Hillside Lot Expensive
meta_description: Why hillside homes cost more to build in Los Angeles: grading, retaining walls, caissons, hillside limits, fire zones and access, and what to check first.
author: Oliver Thornton
body_html:
The Hollywood Hills produce some of the most valuable homes in Los Angeles, and some of the most expensive to build. Two lots with the same view can carry very different costs depending on what is underneath and around them. This guide explains where hillside costs come from and what to check before buying.

Where the Money Goes

Cost driverWhy it adds up
Caissons and foundationsSteep or unstable slopes often need deep drilled piers to reach competent ground
Retaining wallsHolding back hillside soil is structural, engineered and expensive
Grading and haulingMoving earth is limited by ordinance and may require approved haul routes
Geology and soilsReports and city review are required before design is final
AccessNarrow or substandard streets slow deliveries and can trigger fire-access requirements
Fire zone requirementsVery high fire hazard areas carry construction and brush-clearance standards
UtilitiesExtending sewer, water or power up a slope can be costly

The Rules That Shape Hillside Projects

In the City of Los Angeles, the Baseline Hillside Ordinance limits floor area and grading on single-family lots in designated hillside areas, generally based on lot size and slope. Larger grading jobs can require additional approvals, and haul routes may need city sign-off. Most hillside lots also sit in very high fire hazard severity zones, which rules them out of SB 684 entirely.

What Makes a Hillside Lot Worth It

  • An exceptional view that buyers will pay for
  • A naturally flat building pad, so the house sits on the land rather than hanging off it
  • Privacy, without neighboring homes looking down into the yard
  • Good access from a street wide enough for construction and emergency vehicles
  • A reasonable number of levels; homes stacked three or more stories down a slope cost more and sell to a narrower pool

The Lesson We Apply

Steep lots that need extensive retaining walls or caisson work can turn a strong location into a weak project, because the cost lands before anything a buyer will see. That is why, on hillside projects, we look for exceptional views and flat building area, and pass on steep sites, sites without privacy, and designs of three or more levels. See our luxury residential criteria.

Before You Buy a Hillside Lot

  • Get a geology and soils read early, before you commit to a design
  • Check the hillside ordinance limits on floor area and grading for the specific lot
  • Confirm the fire hazard zone and its construction requirements
  • Drive the street with a contractor’s eye for access
  • Price the foundation before you price the finishes

Frequently Asked Questions

Why are hillside homes more expensive to build?
Foundations and earthwork. Steep sites often need deep caisson foundations, retaining walls and extensive grading, plus geology and soils reports, all before the house itself is built.

What is the Baseline Hillside Ordinance?
A City of Los Angeles ordinance that limits floor area and grading on single-family lots in designated hillside areas, generally based on lot size and slope.

Do hillside lots qualify for SB 684?
Rarely. Most Los Angeles hillside lots sit in high or very high fire hazard severity zones, which are excluded from SB 684 and SB 1123.

Which hillside lots work best?
Lots with exceptional views and a naturally flat building pad, good street access, and privacy from neighboring homes.

title: SB 684 vs. SB 1123: What Changed for California Small-Lot Homes
meta_description: A plain-English SB 1123 summary: how it extended SB 684 to vacant single-family lots, what else changed in 2025, and what stayed the same.
author: Oliver Thornton
body_html:
SB 684 created California’s Starter Home Revitalization Act, a ministerial path for subdividing a qualifying lot into as many as ten fee-simple homes. SB 1123, effective July 1, 2025, amended it. If you have read about one and not the other, this summary explains what the second law changed and what it left alone.

The One-Sentence Summary

SB 684 applied the streamlined process to multifamily-zoned land; SB 1123 extended it to vacant lots in single-family zones, refined several standards, and added tenancy in common as a permitted ownership form.

What Changed

TopicSB 684 (original)After SB 1123
Eligible zoningMultifamily zonesAdds vacant lots in single-family zones
Site sizeUp to 5 acresUp to 5 acres (multifamily); 1.5 acres (vacant single-family)
Minimum new lot size600 sq ft600 sq ft (multifamily); 1,200 sq ft (vacant single-family)
Home sizeAverage of 1,750 sq ftClarified as 1,750 net habitable sq ft, with a definition
FrontageLocal minimums limitedMinimum frontage requirements removed
Ownership formsFee simple, CID, co-op, community land trustAdds tenancy in common

What Stayed the Same

  • Ministerial approval. No discretionary hearing and no CEQA review for a qualifying project.
  • The 60-day clock for a decision on a complete application.
  • The 10-lot, 10-home cap, excluding a remainder parcel.
  • Setback and floor-area floors that make compact site plans possible: side and rear setbacks capped at four feet, and floor-area ratio floors of 1.0 or 1.25 depending on the number of homes.
  • Site screens for fire hazard, flood, fault, habitat and contamination, the urban-perimeter test, and the bar on sites already split under SB 9 or the Act.

Why SB 1123 Matters, and Its Limits

SB 1123 opened single-family neighborhoods to small-lot subdivision for the first time, which is a significant expansion of where starter homes can be built. Its main limit is the vacancy requirement: a single-family lot generally has to be empty, or hold only an abandoned and uninhabitable structure, to qualify. A single-family lot with an occupied house on it usually does not. That is why most of the active SB 684 projects on the Westside, including ours, sit on multifamily-zoned lots. For the details, see our SB 1123 requirements guide.

A Note on Later Amendments

The framework is still moving. AB 130 also amended the Act effective July 1, 2025, and local agencies continue to publish their own implementation procedures. Treat any summary, including this one, as a starting point, and confirm the current rules with the city before relying on them.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is SB 1123 a separate law from SB 684?
SB 1123 amended the Starter Home Revitalization Act that SB 684 created. The two work as one framework: SB 684 covers multifamily-zoned land and SB 1123 extends the same process to vacant single-family lots.

When did SB 1123 take effect?
July 1, 2025.

Did SB 1123 change the 10-unit limit?
No. Projects under both remain capped at 10 lots and 10 homes, with an average home size of no more than 1,750 net habitable square feet.

Which is better for a developer, SB 684 or SB 1123?
It depends on zoning and site condition. SB 684 sites are multifamily-zoned and can have an existing house; SB 1123 sites must be vacant single-family lots. Many small-lot developers prefer SB 684 sites because qualifying is more straightforward.

title: TIC vs. Condo in California: How the Two Ownership Types Compare
meta_description: TIC vs. condo in California: what you own, how financing works, HOAs, conversion, resale and risk, explained for buyers, sellers and investors.
author: Oliver Thornton
body_html:
Two people can live in near-identical units in the same building and own them in completely different ways. In California, the two most common shared-building structures are the condominium and the tenancy in common (TIC). They look alike from the street and behave very differently when you finance, sell or manage them.

What You Actually Own

A condo owner holds title to a defined unit, plus a share of the common areas, under a recorded condominium map. A TIC owner holds an undivided fractional interest in the entire property, and a separate co-ownership agreement assigns each owner exclusive use of a particular unit. The difference sounds technical; it drives almost everything else.

Side-by-Side Comparison

CondominiumTenancy in Common
What you ownA defined unit plus a share of common areasA fractional share of the whole property
Recorded mapCondominium map requiredNo condo map
FinancingConventional mortgages widely availableUsually fractional TIC loans from fewer lenders
GovernanceHOA with CC&RsTIC agreement among co-owners
Typical pricingMarket rate for the unitOften a discount to comparable condos
ResaleBroad buyer poolNarrower buyer pool
Shared riskLimited to HOA obligationsCo-owners may share exposure under a blanket loan, if one exists

Financing Is the Big Difference

Because a condo is a separately mapped unit, buyers can use conventional mortgages. A TIC interest usually can’t. Most TIC buyers rely on fractional TIC loans, offered by a smaller group of lenders, which narrows the buyer pool and tends to put TIC prices below comparable condos. That discount is part of what makes TICs an entry point to ownership in expensive markets.

Why TICs Exist in California

Many California buildings can’t easily become condos: conversion may be restricted, a condo map may be impractical, or the timeline too long. A TIC lets owners share a building without a map. In Los Angeles, that has made TIC a common way to sell small multifamily buildings unit by unit to owner-occupants. Our guide to tenancy in common in California and Los Angeles goes deeper.

Where Fee-Simple Small Lots Fit

California’s SB 684 and SB 1123 add a third option on qualifying sites: subdividing the land itself into small fee-simple lots, each with its own parcel number and its own home. Buyers get conventional financing and no shared title, which is why, where a site qualifies, a fee-simple subdivision is generally the stronger exit than either a TIC or a condo. See our SB 684 and SB 1123 guide.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is a TIC cheaper than a condo?
Often, yes. TIC units in California frequently sell below comparable condos, largely because financing options are narrower and resale can take longer.

Can I get a regular mortgage on a TIC?
Usually not a conventional one. Most TIC buyers use a fractional TIC loan from a smaller group of lenders, often with larger down payments and different terms than a conventional mortgage.

Do TICs have HOA dues?
Not in the condominium sense. TIC co-owners share building costs under a tenancy-in-common agreement, which sets out how expenses, use and decisions are handled.

Can a TIC be converted to condos?
Sometimes, depending on local rules. Some cities restrict or regulate condo conversions, so the path varies by jurisdiction and building.

title: The Los Angeles Residential Entitlement Process, Step by Step
meta_description: How residential projects get approved in Los Angeles: ministerial vs. discretionary review, tract maps, plan check and ready-to-issue permits, step by step.
author: Oliver Thornton
body_html:
Before anything is built in Los Angeles, a project has to clear two separate hurdles: entitlement, which decides whether the project is allowed, and permitting, which decides whether the plans are buildable. Understanding the difference explains why some projects start construction in a year and others wait several.

Ministerial vs. Discretionary

The single most important fact about a project is which kind of approval it needs. A ministerial approval is a checklist: if the project meets objective standards, the city must approve it, with no public hearing and no CEQA review. A discretionary approval involves judgment, often a public hearing, environmental review and the possibility of appeal. Laws like SB 684, SB 1123 and SB 9 moved certain housing projects from the second category into the first, which is why they have changed small-lot development.

The Steps

StepWhat happens
1. Due diligenceZoning, lot size, hazards, tenant history and utilities confirmed before or during escrow
2. DesignArchitect prepares the site plan and homes to meet the applicable standards
3. Entitlement applicationSubdivision or zoning application filed; for SB 684, a decision is due within 60 days of a complete application
4. Map approvalTentative tract map approved; conditions issued
5. Plan checkBuilding, fire, utility and other departments review construction drawings, often through several rounds of corrections
6. Ready to issue (RTI)Plan check complete; permits can be pulled once fees are paid
7. ConstructionBuild, inspections and final sign-off
8. Final map and saleFinal map recorded so each new parcel can be sold individually

Where Time Goes

The statutory clocks are short; the real schedule is set by plan check and utility coordination. On the SB 684 projects our team has run in Culver City and Santa Monica, the path from the start of entitlement to ready-to-issue permits has taken about 12 months, trending toward 9–10 months as building departments get familiar with the law. Construction then takes about 12 months. Those are estimates from recent projects, not commitments.

Remodels Are Different

Many remodels and additions need no entitlement at all, only building permits, which is one reason a well-scoped remodel can move faster than a ground-up project. See remodel vs. new construction in Los Angeles.

What Slows Projects Down

  • Incomplete applications that restart the review clock
  • Multiple rounds of plan-check corrections
  • Utility capacity and easement issues
  • Design review boards, historic overlays or coastal review on discretionary projects
  • Tenant-protection issues discovered late in due diligence

Most of these are avoidable with early diligence, which is why we screen zoning, hazards and tenant history before a site goes into contract.

Frequently Asked Questions

What does entitlement mean in real estate?
Entitlement is the process of getting the land-use approvals a project needs before building permits can be issued, such as a subdivision map, a zoning approval or a variance.

What is the difference between ministerial and discretionary approval?
A ministerial approval must be granted if the project meets objective standards, with no public hearing. A discretionary approval involves judgment by decision-makers, often includes public hearings and CEQA review, and can be appealed.

What does RTI mean?
Ready to issue: the point at which plan check is complete and the building permit can be pulled once fees are paid.

How long does entitlement take in Los Angeles?
It varies widely. Discretionary projects can take years. On recent ministerial SB 684 projects, our team has seen about 12 months from the start of entitlement to ready-to-issue permits, trending toward 9 to 10 months.

title: Measure ULA Explained: What LA’s “Mansion Tax” Means for Sellers and Developers
meta_description: Measure ULA explained: which Los Angeles sales it applies to, the 2026 threshold, who pays, and how it is changing what luxury homes get built and sold.
author: Oliver Thornton
body_html:
Measure ULA, approved by Los Angeles voters in November 2022 and in effect since April 1, 2023, added a transfer tax to high-value property sales in the City of Los Angeles. It has quietly reshaped the top of the market, and anyone buying, building or selling a luxury home in the city needs to understand it.

How It Works

  • Where it applies. Sales of property within City of Los Angeles limits. Neighboring cities, including Beverly Hills, Santa Monica and Culver City, are not subject to ULA, though some have transfer taxes of their own.
  • When it applies. When the sale price exceeds the threshold. For sales on or after July 1, 2026, the first threshold is $5,400,000, per the City of Los Angeles Office of Finance. Thresholds adjust each July, and a higher rate applies above a second threshold.
  • How much. The tax is calculated on the entire sale price, not just the amount above the threshold, which creates a steep cliff right at the line.
  • Who pays. Typically the seller, at closing.

The Cliff Effect

Because the tax applies to the full price, a home that sells just over the threshold can net the seller less than one that sells just under it. The result has been a visible cluster of City of Los Angeles sales priced just below the line, and fewer sales just above it. For sellers near the threshold, pricing strategy now matters as much as presentation.

What It Means for Developers

For anyone building to sell in the city, ULA changes the math on the high end. A project designed to resell just above the threshold carries a tax that can erase much of the margin. Many developers, including us, now price City of Los Angeles acquisitions so the finished home will sell below the threshold, and look at higher price points mainly outside city limits, in places like Beverly Hills proper and select Orange County and South Bay markets.

That shift is also part of why small-lot SB 684 homes have become attractive: entry-level fee-simple homes sell far below the ULA threshold, to a much deeper pool of buyers.

Questions to Ask Before You Price a Sale

  • Is the property inside City of Los Angeles limits? Many addresses with a Los Angeles mailing address are not.
  • Which threshold applies on your expected closing date, given the July adjustment?
  • Does pricing just under the threshold net more than pricing just over it?
  • Are there other transfer taxes in your city?

Confirm the current thresholds and rates with the Office of Finance and your tax advisor before relying on them. Measure ULA has been the subject of litigation and proposed changes, and the rules may change.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Measure ULA?
A City of Los Angeles transfer tax approved by voters in 2022 that adds a tax on property sales above a threshold. It took effect on April 1, 2023, and is often called the mansion tax.

What is the Measure ULA threshold in 2026?
For sales on or after July 1, 2026, the first threshold is $5,400,000, according to the City of Los Angeles Office of Finance. The thresholds adjust each July, and a higher rate applies above a second threshold.

Does Measure ULA apply in Beverly Hills or Santa Monica?
No. Measure ULA applies only to sales within City of Los Angeles limits. Other cities, such as Santa Monica, have their own transfer taxes.

Who pays Measure ULA?
It is typically paid by the seller at closing, though the parties can negotiate otherwise.

title: Remodel vs. New Construction in Los Angeles: Why Keeping the Walls Matters
meta_description: Remodel vs. new construction in Los Angeles: how permits, financing, timelines and capital needs differ, and why keeping part of the structure can matter.
author: Oliver Thornton
body_html:
Two projects can produce nearly the same finished house and look completely different to a lender, a building department and a budget. One is a remodel that keeps part of the existing structure; the other is new construction from the ground up. In Los Angeles, that distinction often decides how much capital a project needs and how fast it moves.

How the Two Compare

Remodel / expansionNew construction
ApprovalsOften building permits onlyMay need entitlement plus permits
FinancingRenovation-style loans, usually simplerGround-up construction loans, usually more equity and controls
Capital neededGenerally lowerGenerally higher
ScheduleShorter, defined scopeLonger
Main riskHidden existing conditionsCost and schedule over a longer build

Why Keeping Part of the Structure Matters

When a project retains a meaningful portion of the existing walls or foundation, it can often be permitted and financed as a remodel rather than as new construction. That can reduce the capital a project needs and simplify the approval path. Whether a specific project qualifies depends on the city’s rules and the lender’s policies, so the decision has to be made during design, not after demolition starts.

The Trade-Off: Existing Conditions

Remodels carry a risk ground-up projects don’t: you inherit the house. Foundations, framing, plumbing and electrical only reveal their true condition once the walls are open. Disciplined remodel underwriting carries real contingency in both budget and schedule for exactly that reason.

Where Each Makes Sense

A remodel and expansion fits an under-improved house in a strong neighborhood, especially one with unused floor area or a footprint that can grow. New construction fits when the existing structure is beyond saving, or when the site supports a substantially different product, such as several fee-simple homes under SB 684. On hillside lots, both get harder: steep sites can require retaining walls and caissons that change the economics entirely.

How We Approach It

For luxury single-family projects, we prefer remodels and expansions where part of the existing structure can stay, in Class A, A− and B+ neighborhoods, with a scope we can finish and sell in a defined time frame. We consider ground-up projects selectively and underwrite them more conservatively. See our luxury residential strategy.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is a remodel cheaper than new construction?
Often, but not always. A remodel that keeps part of the structure can reduce demolition, foundation and permitting scope, but hidden conditions can add cost once walls are opened.

How does financing differ for a remodel vs. new construction?
Lenders generally treat a remodel of an existing home as a lower-risk renovation loan, while ground-up construction loans tend to require more equity, more documentation and tighter draw controls.

Does a remodel need entitlement in Los Angeles?
Many remodels and additions need only building permits, not separate entitlement approvals, though hillside, historic or coastal sites can add reviews.

What can go wrong on a remodel?
Scope surprises. Existing conditions only become fully visible once walls are open, so remodels need contingency in both budget and schedule.

title: How Construction Financing Works on an SB 684 Project
meta_description: How lenders size construction loans on SB 684 small-lot projects: as-is entitled value, as-complete value, loan-to-cost and the refinance from acquisition loan.
author: Oliver Thornton
body_html:
Financing is where an SB 684 project either gets easier or stalls. The approval itself creates value, and the way lenders measure that value determines how much new equity a project needs to start construction. This article explains the mechanics in general terms.

Three Stages of Debt

StageTypical loanWhat it funds
AcquisitionShort-term acquisition or bridge loanPurchase of the lot, sometimes with a holdback for design and entitlement
ConstructionConstruction loan, often refinancing the acquisition loanBuilding the homes, with funds drawn as work is completed
SaleLoan repaid home by homeEach closing releases a lot from the loan

What the Appraisal Measures

Construction lenders usually look at two values. The as-is value is what the site is worth today; once a subdivision is approved, that is the value of several entitled lots rather than one older house. The as-complete value is what the finished homes are expected to sell for. Lenders then size the loan against limits such as loan-to-cost (the loan as a share of total project cost) and loan-to-after-repair value (the loan as a share of the as-complete value).

Why Entitlement Can Mean Less Cash at Closing

When the entitled and as-complete values come in well above what was paid for the lot, the construction loan can be large enough to repay the acquisition loan and fund the build without a significant new equity injection. On both SB 684 projects our team has taken to construction financing, the appraisals cleared lenders’ requirements with room to spare and the construction loans closed with no cash required at closing. That is a financing milestone, not a finished result: no SB 684 project in our pipeline has completed its sellout yet.

What Lenders Look For

  • An approved tentative tract map and a clear path to ready-to-issue permits
  • A credible construction budget and schedule, with contingency
  • Comparable sales supporting the as-complete value of each home
  • Sponsor experience building comparable product
  • Personal guarantees from the sponsor’s principals, which are common on construction loans

The Risks

Appraisals are opinions, not promises. Costs can rise, schedules can slip, interest can accrue faster than planned, and finished homes can sell for less or more slowly than expected. Leverage that helps when values hold can hurt when they don’t. Anyone evaluating a project should look at the downside case as carefully as the appraisal. See our risks and disclosures and how we work with investors.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why does entitlement change a project's value?
Approval turns one lot into several legal, buildable lots. Appraisers can then value the site as entitled land and the finished homes individually, which is often well above the value of the original lot.

What is loan-to-after-repair value (LTARV)?
The loan amount divided by the appraised value of the completed project. Lenders use it, alongside loan-to-cost, to size construction loans.

What does no cash to close mean on a construction refinance?
That the new construction loan was large enough to repay the acquisition loan and cover closing costs without the borrower bringing new money to closing.

Is the outcome of an SB 684 project guaranteed by its appraisal?
No. Appraisals are estimates. Construction costs, schedules and sale prices can differ from projections, and no project's financing guarantees its results.

title: SB 684 vs. SB 9: Which California Lot-Split Law Fits Your Site?
meta_description: SB 684 vs. SB 9 compared: units allowed, zoning, owner-occupancy, tenant rules and approval paths, and which California lot-split law fits a given site.
author: Oliver Thornton
body_html:
California now has two ministerial paths for turning one residential lot into several homes: SB 9, in effect since 2022, and the Starter Home Revitalization Act created by SB 684 and extended by SB 1123. Both skip the discretionary hearing. They are built for very different projects, and picking the wrong one can cap a site well below what it could carry.

This guide compares the two side by side from the perspective of a developer running SB 684 projects on the Westside. For the full rules on SB 684 and SB 1123, see our complete SB 684 and SB 1123 guide.

The Short Answer

SB 9 is a homeowner’s tool: split a single-family lot in two, add a unit or two, and keep living there. SB 684 and SB 1123 are a small-builder’s tool: subdivide a qualifying lot into as many as ten fee-simple parcels and build a new home on each, sold one by one to owner-occupants. If the goal is a small community of new starter homes, the Starter Home Revitalization Act is the path. If the goal is one or two extra units behind an existing house, SB 9 usually is.

Side-by-Side Comparison

SB 684 / SB 1123SB 9
ZoningMultifamily zones (SB 684); vacant single-family lots (SB 1123)Single-family zones
Maximum new lotsUp to 102
Maximum homesUp to 10Up to 4 (2 per lot)
Site size limit5 acres (multifamily) / 1.5 acres (vacant single-family)None stated; each new lot generally at least 1,200 sq ft
Owner-occupancyNot requiredApplicant affidavit to occupy one unit for 3 years (lot splits)
ApprovalMinisterial; no hearing, no CEQA; 60-day decisionMinisterial; no hearing
Typical buyerOwner-occupants buying new fee-simple homesThe existing owner, or a buyer of one split parcel
Prior splitsNot allowed if previously split under SB 9 or the SHRANot allowed on a parcel created by a prior SB 9 split

Where SB 9 Fits

SB 9 works best for an owner who wants to stay. Splitting a large single-family lot in two, keeping the existing house and adding a second home on the new parcel can unlock value without selling. Because a lot split generally requires the applicant to commit to living there for three years, SB 9 is rarely a practical route for a developer building to sell, and its four-unit ceiling limits how much new housing a site can deliver.

Where SB 684 and SB 1123 Fit

The Starter Home Revitalization Act was written for exactly the project SB 9 can’t do well: a builder subdividing an infill lot into several small fee-simple parcels and selling each new home individually. SB 684 covers multifamily-zoned land; SB 1123, effective July 1, 2025, extends the same process to vacant single-family lots. Lot-size, setback and floor-area floors set by the state make compact site plans possible, and the 60-day ministerial decision turns entitlement into a schedule rather than a political outcome.

On the Westside, that is how a dated house on a 6,000-square-foot multifamily lot can become six new homes, each on its own parcel and each financeable with a conventional mortgage.

Tenant and Demolition Rules

Both laws protect existing renters, and both screen out sites that were recently taken off the rental market. In practice, the sites that work best for SB 684 are owner-occupied homes or homes with no rental history in the last five years, with no Ellis Act withdrawal in the last fifteen. A site that fails those screens may not qualify at all, so tenant history is one of the first things a developer will ask about.

Which Is Better for an Owner Selling a Lot?

If you plan to sell rather than build, the question is which law makes your lot most valuable to a buyer. A multifamily-zoned lot that can carry six or more fee-simple homes under SB 684 is often worth more to a small-lot developer than to a buyer valuing only the existing house, because the price is set by what the land can become. Our guide to selling your lot to an SB 684 developer walks through how that pricing works.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I use SB 684 and SB 9 on the same lot?
No. A lot that has already been split under SB 9 or under the Starter Home Revitalization Act is not eligible for another split under SB 684 or SB 1123, so the pathway has to be chosen before the first application.

How many homes can I build under SB 9 vs. SB 684?
SB 9 allows up to four units: a lot split into two parcels with up to two units on each. SB 684 and SB 1123 allow up to ten lots and ten homes on a qualifying site.

Does SB 9 require the owner to live on the property?
For an SB 9 urban lot split, the applicant generally has to sign an affidavit stating they intend to live in one of the units for at least three years. SB 684 and SB 1123 have no owner-occupancy requirement, which is one reason developers use them.

Which law applies to multifamily-zoned lots?
SB 684. SB 9 applies to single-family zones, and SB 1123 extends the SB 684 process to vacant single-family-zoned lots.

title: SB 1123 Lot Split Requirements: Up to 10 Homes on a Single-Family Lot
meta_description: SB 1123 requirements: which single-family lots qualify, what counts as vacant, lot and unit limits, setbacks, parking and the 60-day ministerial approval.
author: Oliver Thornton
body_html:
SB 1123 took the streamlined subdivision process that SB 684 created for multifamily land and extended it to vacant lots in single-family zones, effective July 1, 2025. On a qualifying site, an owner or developer can create up to ten small fee-simple lots and build a home on each, approved ministerially with no public hearing and no CEQA review.

This guide summarizes the requirements a single-family-zoned site has to meet. It is general information, not legal advice; local agencies implement the law through their own procedures, and the statute has already been amended once.

Requirements at a Glance

RequirementSB 1123 (vacant single-family lots)
ZoningSingle-family residential zone
Site conditionVacant (see below)
Maximum site size1.5 acres
Maximum lots and homes10 lots, 10 dwelling units
Minimum new lot size1,200 sq ft
Average home sizeNo more than 1,750 net habitable sq ft
Side and rear setbacksCapped at 4 ft from the original lot line
Lot width, depth, frontageNo local minimum may be imposed
ParkingNo more than 1 space per home; none near qualifying transit
Ownership formsFee simple, common interest development, co-op, community land trust or tenancy in common
ApprovalMinisterial; decision within 60 days of a complete application

What Counts as Vacant

The single biggest gate in SB 1123 is that the lot must be vacant. Under the statute, a lot can qualify if it has no permanent structure, or if its only permanent structure is abandoned and uninhabitable. A single-family lot with an occupied house on it generally does not qualify under SB 1123. That is the main reason developers on this pathway prefer multifamily-zoned lots under SB 684, where an existing house does not disqualify the site.

Site Exclusions

Like SB 684, SB 1123 screens out sites with environmental or safety constraints. A qualifying site generally cannot be in a high or very high fire hazard severity zone, an earthquake fault zone, a special flood hazard area or regulatory floodway, wetlands, protected species habitat, a hazardous waste site, or land under a conservation easement. At least 75 percent of the site’s perimeter must adjoin parcels developed with urban uses, and the site must be served by public water and sewer. A lot previously split under SB 9 or the Starter Home Revitalization Act is not eligible.

In Los Angeles, the fire hazard screen alone rules out most hillside lots, which is why SB 1123 projects concentrate in the flats.

Standards a City Can’t Exceed

The law limits what a local agency can require. Side and rear setbacks are capped at four feet from the original lot line, no separation is required between homes beyond building-code minimums, and a city cannot impose minimum lot width, depth or frontage. Floor-area limits cannot be set below a floor-area ratio of 1.0 for three to seven homes or 1.25 for eight to ten. Those floors are what make a ten-home plan possible on a lot a conventional subdivision would treat as one house.

What Makes an SB 1123 Site Work for a Developer

Qualifying is not the same as penciling. A small-lot developer will look for a site large enough for at least six homes, in a neighborhood where new starter homes sell well, with simple access and flat grades. Corner and street-to-alley lots are easier to plan. Because SB 1123 sites must be vacant, they are rarer than SB 684 sites, and they are worth flagging when you find one. If you own or represent a vacant single-family lot that might qualify, send it to us for a quick read.

Frequently Asked Questions

When did SB 1123 take effect?
July 1, 2025. It amended the Starter Home Revitalization Act created by SB 684.

Does SB 1123 apply to a lot with a house on it?
SB 1123 applies to vacant lots in single-family zones. A lot can count as vacant if it has no permanent structure, or if its only permanent structure is abandoned and uninhabitable. A lot with an occupied house generally does not qualify under SB 1123, though a multifamily-zoned lot with a house may qualify under SB 684.

How big can an SB 1123 site be?
No more than 1.5 acres, and the project can create no more than 10 lots and 10 homes.

What is the minimum lot size under SB 1123?
New lots created on a vacant single-family site must be at least 1,200 square feet.

title: Selling Your Lot to an SB 684 Developer: What Owners and Agents Should Know
meta_description: How SB 684 changes what a Los Angeles lot is worth, how developers price land by the number of homes, what qualifies, and what to send for a fast answer.
author: Oliver Thornton
body_html:
California’s SB 684 quietly changed what a lot of Los Angeles land is worth. A dated house on a multifamily-zoned lot used to be valued like any other house. Today, if that lot can be subdivided into six or more fee-simple homes, its value to the right buyer is set by what it can become. This guide is for owners, listing agents and wholesalers deciding whether a property is worth showing to an SB 684 developer.

Why SB 684 Changed What Your Lot Is Worth

Under SB 684, a qualifying lot can be split into as many as ten parcels and approved ministerially, with no hearing and no CEQA review. Each new parcel gets its own APN and a new home that sells individually to an owner-occupant. A developer looking at your lot is really looking at those future homes, so the more homes the site can carry, and the stronger the neighborhood they will sell in, the more the land is worth.

Does My Lot Qualify? A Quick Screen

Final eligibility depends on the local agency, but most of the screen can be done in a few minutes:

  • Location. An infill lot in the flats. We focus on Westside neighborhoods such as Culver City, Santa Monica, Mar Vista, Palms, Del Rey, West Los Angeles and Westchester, plus select coastal markets.
  • Size. At least 5,000 square feet, ideally 6,000 or more. The bigger the lot, the more homes it can carry.
  • Homes. Room for at least six fee-simple homes, each with at least one parking space.
  • Zoning. Multifamily zoning is preferred. A single-family lot can qualify under SB 1123 only if it is vacant.
  • Shape. Corner and street-to-alley lots are preferred; mid-block lots can still work.
  • Tenant history. Owner-occupied, or no rental history in the last five years, and no Ellis Act filing in the last fifteen.
  • Hazards. Not in a high or very high fire hazard severity zone, and clear of the law’s other site exclusions.

How Developers Price SB 684 Land

Price follows the number of homes a site can carry and what each will sell for. As a rough guide to how we buy:

Homes the site can carryTypical purchase price
6 homes$800,000 – $1,500,000
8 homes$1,500,000 – $2,200,000
10 homes$2,000,000 – $3,000,000

These are typical ranges, not limits. The stronger the neighborhood and the higher each finished home will sell for, the more a developer can pay. On the Westside, recent SB 684 acquisitions in Culver City have closed in the $1,150,000 to $1,410,000 range for five- and six-home sites; you can see them on our Submit a Deal page.

What to Send for a Fast Answer

Only the address and your contact details are required, but the more you share, the faster you get a real answer:

  • Address and APN
  • Lot size and zoning, if known
  • Asking price, or the contract price and assignment terms for wholesale deals
  • Occupancy and tenant history over the last five years
  • Photos, a survey, or any plans already in progress

What Happens After You Submit

We review the site, zoning and comparable sales, and within two business days you get a yes, a no, or our questions. If it fits, we walk the property and make an offer. When the deal calls for it we can close quickly with cash or private financing, and we work with listing and buyer’s agents on both sides and honor the agreed commission.

For Agents and Wholesalers

If you see older homes on large multifamily-zoned lots in your farm area, you are looking at potential SB 684 sites. Many owners don’t know what their land is worth under the new law. Bringing us a qualifying property, on or off market, is often the fastest way to a clean sale. Submit a property here.

Frequently Asked Questions

What makes a lot attractive to an SB 684 developer?
An infill lot of at least 5,000 square feet, ideally 6,000 or more, in a strong neighborhood, zoned for multifamily, with room for at least six fee-simple homes, no tenant history in the last five years and no Ellis Act withdrawal in the last fifteen.

How do SB 684 developers price land?
By what the site can become: the number of homes it can carry and what each finished home is likely to sell for, rather than the value of the existing house alone.

Do you pay agent commissions?
Yes. Assemble Capital works with listing and buyer's agents and honors the agreed commission.

Do you buy from wholesalers?
Yes. Send the contract price and your assignment terms with the property details.

title: Passive Real Estate Investing: How It Actually Works
meta_description: What passive real estate investing means, the four main routes — REITs, crowdfunding, private funds and syndications — how they differ on liquidity and minimums, and what you give up.
author: Oliver Thornton
body_html:
Passive real estate investing means owning a share of real property without running it. Someone else finds the deal, arranges the debt, manages the construction or the tenants, and eventually sells. You supply capital and receive your share of whatever the project produces.

The word does a lot of work, and not all of it honest. “Passive” describes your workload, not your risk. It does not mean safe, it does not mean liquid, and it does not mean returns arrive on a schedule. This guide covers what the term actually means, the four main ways to do it, where private syndication fits among them, and what you give up in exchange for not doing the work.

What is passive real estate investing?

The distinction is control. An active investor buys a duplex, finds the tenants, takes the 11pm call about the water heater, and decides when to sell. A passive investor commits capital to a vehicle run by someone else and has no operational role and, generally, no decision-making authority.

That is the trade at the centre of every option below: you give up control, and in return you give up the work. Whether that is a good trade depends less on the asset than on who is doing the work in your place.

The Four Main Ways to Invest Passively

What it isLiquidityTypical minimumWho can invest
Public REITsShares in a listed company that owns income propertyDaily, on an exchangePrice of one shareAnyone
Crowdfunding platformsOnline marketplaces offering fractional positions in deals or fundsLimited; often none until exitLow — often hundreds to low thousandsVaries; some accredited-only
Private fundsA pooled vehicle investing across many assets, often blind poolNone until the fund winds downSubstantialGenerally accredited
SyndicationsA single identified property, financed by a group of investors for that dealNone until that property sells or refinancesSubstantialGenerally accredited

These are genuinely different products, not tiers of the same one.

REITs are the most liquid and the least differentiated. You get diversified exposure to institutional-grade property, you can sell on a Tuesday, and you also get equity-market volatility: listed REITs trade on sentiment as well as on the buildings they own.

Crowdfunding platforms lowered the minimum dramatically, which is a real democratisation. What they did not lower is the diligence burden. The platform is a marketplace; the person actually running your money is the sponsor behind the individual deal, and platform quality and sponsor quality are separate questions.

Funds ask you to underwrite a manager and a strategy rather than a building, because at the time you commit, the assets may not have been bought yet. That is the blind-pool trade: diversification in exchange for not knowing exactly what you own.

Syndications are the opposite. One identified property, one business plan, one exit. You can inspect the actual asset before committing, and you carry concentrated exposure to it.

Where Syndication Fits — And Where It Doesn’t

A syndication suits an investor who wants to see the specific thing they are buying, is comfortable with capital committed for years, and would rather concentrate into a few deals they can evaluate than spread thinly across a portfolio someone else assembles.

It is a poor fit for an investor who may need the money back, who wants to invest small amounts across many assets, or who does not want to evaluate a sponsor. That last one matters most, and it is the part people skip. In a syndication you are not really buying a building — you are buying a sponsor’s execution of a plan for a building. The building is visible in the offering documents. The execution is not, which is why the sponsor’s track record does more work in the decision than the property photographs.

What “Passive” Actually Means Inside a Syndication

Most syndications are structured with a general partner and limited partners. The general partner (the sponsor) sources the deal, arranges financing, executes the business plan and handles reporting. Limited partners contribute capital and hold a passive stake — and their limited liability is precisely why they cannot take an operational role. Passivity is a legal feature of the structure, not just a lifestyle preference. We cover the split in detail in the general partner versus limited partner guide.

In practice, a limited partner's obligations are: perform diligence before committing, fund the capital call, read the reporting, and handle the tax documents. What they do not get is a vote on the roof contractor, the listing price, or the timing of the sale.

What You Give Up

An honest account of the costs, because they are not always stated plainly:

  • Liquidity. This is the big one. Private real estate positions generally cannot be sold when you want out. Capital is committed for the life of the project, and business plans slip. Money you may need is not money for this.
  • Control. You cannot overrule a decision you disagree with. If the sponsor is wrong, you are wrong with them.
  • Transparency between reports. You know what the sponsor tells you, at the cadence they tell you. A sponsor's reporting discipline in a bad quarter is worth more than their pitch in a good one.
  • Certainty of distributions. Projected distributions are projections. Development projects in particular may produce nothing at all until an exit.
  • Simplicity at tax time. Partnership investments generally produce a K-1 rather than a 1099, and K-1s often arrive later than you would like.

None of these are reasons not to invest. They are reasons to size the position properly and to be honest with yourself about the money you are committing.

How to Evaluate a Passive Opportunity

The instinct is to start with the projected return. That is the least reliable number in the document, because it is the one the sponsor chose. Better questions, roughly in order:

  • Who is the sponsor, and what have they finished? Completed projects across a full cycle, not deals in progress during a rising market.
  • How is the deal structured? Where investor capital sits relative to the sponsor’s, and what has to happen before the sponsor participates in profit. Structure outlasts projections.
  • What does the sponsor have at stake? Capital alongside yours, personal guarantees on the debt, or fees deferred behind your return are all ways a sponsor carries real exposure.
  • What is the downside case? Not the base case — what happens if the timeline slips and the exit price is lower. Downside protection is where underwriting quality shows.
  • What does the paperwork actually say? The offering memorandum and operating agreement govern, not the summary deck. Read the offering memorandum and know the red flags.

Who can invest passively in private real estate?

REITs are open to anyone. Most private syndications and funds are offered under exemptions that limit participation to accredited investors — and in some offerings, a limited number of sophisticated non-accredited investors. Accreditation is defined by the SEC on income, net worth, or professional credentials; we set out the current thresholds in the accredited investor requirements guide.

Two mechanics worth knowing. Under Rule 506(b), a sponsor cannot advertise the offering publicly and relies on investor self-certification, which is why these deals reach people through existing relationships rather than advertisements. Under Rule 506(c), a sponsor may market publicly but must take reasonable steps to verify accreditation — typically documentation from your accountant or attorney rather than a checkbox.

Is passive real estate investing worth it?

It depends on what you are comparing it to and what you need from the money.

Against active ownership, passive investing trades control and a meaningful share of the upside for not doing the work — a good trade if your time is worth more elsewhere, a poor one if you enjoy the work and would have done it well.

Against public markets, private real estate trades liquidity for the possibility of returns uncorrelated with equities. Whether that premium is real depends almost entirely on the operator, which is why the diligence above is not optional.

What passive investing is not, in any version, is a way to avoid thinking. The work moves from managing property to selecting people.

Working With Assemble Capital

Assemble Capital is a Los Angeles real estate syndication and development firm pursuing value-add and opportunistic residential projects — SB 684 fee-simple subdivisions, luxury residential development, multifamily and tenancy-in-common housing — and syndicates those projects with investors who hold passive stakes. The work is carried in-house rather than brokered out, and the principals personally guarantee the loans on every deal. Investors never sign personal guarantees on project financing. You can read the four strategies we run or what we have completed.

If you are an accredited investor evaluating passive real estate and want to see how we underwrite, get in touch. Assemble Capital offerings are made only to accredited and otherwise eligible investors, and only through definitive offering documents — nothing on this page is an offer, a solicitation, or a recommendation to invest.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is passive real estate investing?
Passive real estate investing means owning a share of real property without operating it. A sponsor, manager or company handles acquisition, financing, management and sale, while the investor contributes capital and holds a non-operational stake. Common forms include REITs, crowdfunding platforms, private funds and syndications.

How do you invest in real estate passively?
The four main routes are public REITs bought through a brokerage, online crowdfunding platforms, private real estate funds, and syndications of individual properties. They differ substantially in liquidity, minimum investment and who is eligible to participate.

Is passive real estate investing actually passive?
The ongoing management is, but the selection is not. Private investments are illiquid and generally cannot be exited early, so the diligence has to happen before committing rather than after. The work shifts from managing property to evaluating sponsors and documents.

How much money do you need to invest passively in real estate?
It varies enormously by route. A REIT share can cost less than a hundred dollars; crowdfunding minimums are often in the hundreds or low thousands; private funds and syndications typically require substantially more and are usually limited to accredited investors. Specific minimums are set by each individual offering.

Do you have to be accredited to invest in real estate passively?
Not for REITs, and not for every crowdfunding offering. Most private syndications and funds rely on exemptions that limit participation to accredited investors, though some permit a limited number of sophisticated non-accredited investors.

What is the difference between a REIT and a syndication?
A REIT is a company holding a diversified portfolio, usually publicly traded and sellable on any market day. A syndication is a private group investment in one identified property, with capital committed until that property is sold or refinanced. REITs offer liquidity and diversification; syndications offer a specific, inspectable asset and concentrated exposure to it.

What are the risks of passive real estate investing?
Illiquidity, loss of control over decisions, dependence on the sponsor's execution, leverage, and the possibility of losing some or all of the investment. Projected distributions are projections, not obligations, and development projects may produce no income before exit.

Sources and Review

Accredited investor standards are set by the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission under Regulation D; thresholds and the offering mechanics of Rule 506(b) and Rule 506(c) are described in the SEC's published guidance and are subject to change. Minimums, liquidity terms and eligibility described here are general market practice and vary by individual offering.

This article is general educational information, not investment, legal or tax advice, and not an offer or solicitation of any investment. Private real estate investments are speculative, illiquid, and involve risk including possible loss of the entire investment. Consult your own financial, legal and tax advisors before making any investment decision.

title: Tenancy in Common in California & Los Angeles, Explained
meta_description: What a TIC property is, why tenancy in common is common in Los Angeles, how TIC compares to a condo and to joint tenancy, and how fractional TIC financing works.
author: Oliver Thornton
body_html:
In most of the country, if you want to sell the units of a small apartment building to individual homeowners, you convert it to condominiums. In Los Angeles, for a large share of the existing stock, you cannot. Tenancy in common — TIC — is the structure that fills that gap, and it is why a form of ownership that is a curiosity elsewhere is a working strategy here.

This guide covers what a TIC property actually is, why it exists in Los Angeles specifically, how it compares to a condominium, how buyers finance one, and where the structure is the right tool rather than a workaround. It is written from the perspective of a developer who underwrites and executes these projects, not a general explainer.

What is a TIC property?

A tenancy in common is a form of co-ownership. Each owner holds an undivided fractional interest in the entire property — not a deeded box of airspace — and a separate written agreement gives each owner the exclusive right to occupy a specific unit.

That distinction is the whole thing. A condominium buyer owns a legally separate parcel with its own assessor's parcel number. A TIC buyer owns a percentage of one undivided parcel, plus a contractual right to live in unit 2. The building is never legally subdivided; the rights are allocated by contract instead.

Everything else follows from that. The TIC agreement is not boilerplate — it is the operating document that defines occupancy rights, how the mortgage and property taxes are allocated, how expenses and reserves are shared, what happens when someone wants to sell, and how disputes get resolved. In a condominium, most of that is handled by statute and a recorded declaration. In a TIC, it is handled by the agreement, which is why the quality of the document matters more than buyers usually expect.

Why TIC Exists in Los Angeles

TIC is not popular in Los Angeles because it is elegant. It is popular because the alternative is frequently unavailable.

Converting an existing rental building to condominiums is a subdivision. It requires a map under the Subdivision Map Act and it runs through a discretionary local process — and Los Angeles layers additional restrictions on top of that, particularly where the building contains units subject to the Rent Stabilization Ordinance. For much of the older small-multifamily stock, condominium conversion is either legally closed or so slow and uncertain that no one underwrites it.

A TIC is not a subdivision. No new parcels are created, so no map is required. That is the entire structural advantage: TIC reaches the for-sale buyer in buildings that cannot be condo-mapped.

Two cautions belong here, and they are the ones most often skipped. First, tenant protections do not evaporate because the ownership form changed — buildings with rent-stabilized tenants carry obligations that survive a sale, and clearing occupancy is governed by state and local law, including the Ellis Act where it applies. Second, several California jurisdictions regulate TIC conversions directly. These rules change, and they differ block to block. Any specific building needs current advice from qualified California real estate counsel before anyone assumes a TIC exit is available.

TIC vs. Condo: What Actually Differs

CondominiumTenancy in Common
What you ownA separate legal parcel (your unit) plus a share of common areaAn undivided percentage of the whole property
Assessor's parcel numberIndividual APN per unitOne APN for the entire building
Requires a subdivision mapYesNo
Governing documentRecorded CC&Rs, governed largely by statuteThe TIC agreement, governed largely by contract
Occupancy rightBy deedBy written agreement among owners
Typical financingConventional, conforming-eligibleFractional TIC loan from a portfolio lender
Property taxesBilled individuallyOne bill, allocated by agreement
Buyer pool at resaleBroadNarrower — limited to buyers and lenders who transact in TIC

The honest summary: a condominium is the cleaner asset, and where a condo map is genuinely available it is usually the better outcome. TIC earns its place where that option is closed.

TIC vs. Joint Tenancy: How Title Is Actually Held

Tenancy in common is one of several ways two or more people can hold title to California real property. The comparison that matters most — and the one people most often get wrong — is against joint tenancy. The difference is not cosmetic. It determines what happens to an owner's share when they die, and whether shares have to be equal.

Tenancy in CommonJoint Tenancy
Ownership sharesCan be unequal — 60/40, 25/25/50, any splitMust be equal
Right of survivorshipNoYes
On an owner's deathThe share passes through their will or estateThe share passes automatically to the surviving joint tenants
Transferring a shareAn owner may sell or transfer their interestA transfer generally severs the joint tenancy as to that share
When acquiredOwners can acquire interests at different timesTraditionally requires the interests be created at the same time, in the same instrument
Typical useUnrelated co-owners; investment and for-sale housingMarried couples and family members holding a home together

Does tenancy in common have right of survivorship? No. That single fact is the practical dividing line. When a joint tenant dies, their interest passes automatically to the surviving joint tenants, outside probate. When a tenant in common dies, nothing passes automatically — the interest is part of their estate and goes wherever their will or California's intestate succession rules send it.

For a for-sale housing project, that is a feature rather than a drawback. TIC buyers are unrelated parties who want their own inheritable asset, not one that reverts to their neighbours. Unequal shares matter for the same reason: a two-bedroom unit and a studio in the same building are not worth the same, and TIC percentages are set to reflect that. Joint tenancy cannot express it.

California also recognises community property and community property with right of survivorship for married couples, which carry tax treatment that neither TIC nor joint tenancy provides. How any individual buyer should take title is a question for their own attorney and tax advisor — it depends on their marital status, estate plan, and who else is on the loan.

How Tenants in Common Hold Title in California

In California, a deed conveying property to two or more people who are not married is presumed to create a tenancy in common unless it expressly says otherwise. Joint tenancy has to be stated. That default is why TIC turns up so often in California title work without anyone having deliberately chosen it.

In a structured TIC project the choice is deliberate, and the percentages, occupancy rights and transfer rules are set out in the TIC agreement rather than left to the default. That is the difference between two friends who happen to hold title as tenants in common and a professionally structured building — not the form of ownership, but whether the agreement behind it was drafted to be lived in, financed, and eventually sold.

How TIC Financing Works

This is the question that decides whether a TIC project is executable, and the answer has changed materially in the last decade.

Historically, TIC buyers had two options: pay cash, or take a shared blanket loan in which every owner sat on a single mortgage against the whole building. The blanket structure created the obvious problem — each owner's credit exposure was tied to every other owner's ability to pay. One default became everyone's problem. That risk kept the structure marginal.

Fractional TIC financing changed that. Multiple lenders now write individual loans secured against an individual TIC interest, so each owner has their own mortgage, their own rate, and their own obligation. That is what makes TIC executable at scale rather than a niche cash-buyer product.

What buyers should still expect, relative to a conventional mortgage on a condominium:

  • Portfolio products, not conforming loans. Fractional TIC loans are held by the originating lender rather than sold to Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac, so terms are set by that lender rather than by agency guidelines.
  • A smaller lender set. A handful of specialists write this paper in California, not every bank.
  • Pricing and down payment that reflect the above. Terms are generally less favorable than a conforming loan on a comparable condominium.
  • Underwriting of the TIC agreement itself. Lenders review the document, not only the borrower. A poorly drafted agreement can make a building unfinanceable.

For a developer, that last point is the operational one. The TIC agreement is drafted long before the first unit is marketed, and it determines which lenders will lend in the building at all.

The Tradeoff Nobody Should Skip: Absorption

A bulk sale is one transaction with one buyer. A TIC sellout is several transactions with several buyers, each securing their own financing on their own timeline, from a buyer pool that is narrower than the condominium market by construction.

That takes time, and time is the cost of the structure. A project underwritten on aggregate unit value but financed on a schedule that assumes a bulk-sale timeline is a project with a problem. The disciplined version sets the bulk-sale fallback value, the lender's partial-release terms, and the absorption assumption before acquisition — not after the first unit sits.

Where TIC Is the Right Tool — And Where It Isn't

TIC is a structure for a specific situation: a small building whose units are worth materially more sold individually than the whole is worth sold to an investor, in a case where the building cannot be condo-mapped.

The economics come from who is bidding. An investor buying a three-unit building prices it on income — rents, expenses, a cap rate. Three separate homebuyers price the same square footage as places to live. On small buildings that spread is real, and capturing it is the entire thesis.

Where TIC is not the answer is equally important. If a site can be subdivided into fee-simple parcels, it generally should be. Fee-simple lots get individual APNs, individual APNs get conventional mortgages, and conventional mortgages get the widest buyer pool. That is why SB 684 and SB 1123 matter: on a qualifying site they make a fee-simple subdivision ministerially approvable, and electing TIC on such a site would trade a stronger exit for a weaker one. SB 1123 permits tenancy in common as an ownership form — but permitted is not the same as optimal.

The rule of thumb: subdivide when you can, TIC when you can't.

How TIC Units Are Actually Sold in Los Angeles

Two different sales happen in a TIC project, and it is worth keeping them apart. The units are sold to individual homebuyers — that is the exit. The investment in the project is a separate matter, offered privately to eligible investors under securities law. This section is about the first.

TIC units in Los Angeles are marketed much like any other for-sale home. They are listed on the MLS, shown at open houses, and bought by owner-occupants rather than investors — which is the entire point, since the homebuyer bid is what exceeds the cap-rate bid. What differs is the disclosure and financing work sitting behind the listing.

In practice, a few things shape how these sales run:

  • Pricing sits between two reference points. Comparable condominiums set the ceiling, because a TIC generally trades at some discount to an equivalent condo to compensate for the financing and liquidity differences. The building's bulk investor value sets the floor. The strategy lives in that band, and where a particular unit lands depends on the submarket, the quality of the finish, and how well the TIC agreement reads to a lender.
  • The buyer needs a lender who writes fractional loans. Not every mortgage broker has placed one. Sellers of TIC units typically identify lenders in advance so buyers are not left to discover the constraint mid-escrow.
  • The TIC agreement goes out with the disclosures. Buyers — and their lenders and attorneys — read it. A document that allocates costs unclearly, or restricts transfer awkwardly, will show up as a financing problem rather than a legal one.
  • Units generally release in sequence rather than all at once. Releasing gradually lets pricing respond to real demand instead of guessing at it, and it keeps the partial-release terms of the project debt manageable.
  • Absorption sets the pace. Each unit waits on its own buyer securing their own financing. A three or four unit building sells over a window measured in many months, not weeks.

The operational discipline is unglamorous and it is most of the work: having the agreement drafted to be financeable before marketing begins, having lender relationships established rather than hoped for, and holding a bulk-sale fallback that is underwritten rather than assumed.

What This Means for Los Angeles Small Multifamily

Los Angeles has a deep inventory of two-to-four-unit buildings, much of it older, much of it in neighborhoods where a homebuyer will pay a premium a cap-rate buyer will not. For the portion of that stock where condominium conversion is closed, TIC is the only structure that reaches the for-sale buyer at all.

That is a durable niche rather than a large one. It rewards operators who have run the process before — because the difficulty is not the concept, it is the sequencing: the agreement drafted to be financeable, the lender relationships established before marketing, the tenant and regulatory position confirmed at acquisition rather than discovered later, and the fallback underwritten from day one.

Working With Assemble Capital

Assemble Capital acquires small multifamily buildings in Los Angeles and executes exactly the strategy described here — structuring the tenancy in common, drafting the agreement to be financeable, lining up fractional lenders before marketing, and underwriting the bulk-sale fallback from the outset. We syndicate those projects with investors, and the principals personally guarantee the loans on every deal; investors never sign personal guarantees on the financing. You can read how we approach the strategy or what we have completed.

If you are an accredited investor and want to understand how we underwrite and structure these projects, get in touch. Assemble Capital offerings are made only to accredited and otherwise eligible investors, and only through definitive offering documents — nothing on this page is an offer, a solicitation, or a recommendation to invest.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is a TIC property?
A tenancy-in-common property is one owned by two or more parties, each holding an undivided fractional interest in the whole property rather than a separately deeded unit. A written TIC agreement gives each owner the exclusive right to occupy a specific unit.

What is the difference between a TIC and a condo?
A condominium unit is its own legal parcel with its own assessor's parcel number, created through a subdivision map. A TIC is one undivided parcel in which owners hold percentage interests, with occupancy allocated by contract. Condos finance conventionally; TICs use fractional loans from portfolio lenders.

Why is TIC so common in Los Angeles?
Because condominium conversion of existing rental buildings is heavily restricted, particularly where units are subject to the Rent Stabilization Ordinance. A TIC is not a subdivision and requires no map, so it can reach for-sale buyers in buildings that cannot legally be condo-mapped.

Can you get a mortgage on a TIC in California?
Yes. Several California lenders write fractional TIC loans secured against an individual interest, so each owner carries their own mortgage rather than sharing a blanket loan. These are portfolio products rather than conforming loans, and terms are generally less favorable than a conventional mortgage on a comparable condominium.

Is a TIC a good investment?
That depends entirely on the specific building, its price relative to comparable condominiums, the quality of the TIC agreement, and which lenders will finance in it. TIC interests are less liquid than condominiums and sell into a narrower buyer pool. This article is educational and is not investment advice.

Do TIC owners share one property tax bill?
Generally yes. The property has a single assessor's parcel number, so one tax bill is issued and allocated among owners according to the TIC agreement.

What happens if a TIC owner wants to sell?
The TIC agreement governs. Most agreements permit an owner to sell their interest and the right to occupy their unit, often subject to notice provisions or a right of first refusal. The practical constraint is the buyer pool: the purchaser must be willing to buy a TIC interest and able to finance it.

Does tenancy in common have right of survivorship?
No. Tenancy in common does not carry a right of survivorship. When a tenant in common dies, their interest becomes part of their estate and passes under their will or by intestate succession, rather than automatically to the other owners. Joint tenancy is the form that carries survivorship.

What is the difference between joint tenancy and tenancy in common?
Joint tenancy requires equal shares and carries a right of survivorship, so a deceased owner's interest passes automatically to the surviving joint tenants. Tenancy in common allows unequal shares, has no survivorship, and lets each owner leave their interest to whomever they choose. Joint tenancy is typical for married couples; tenancy in common is typical for unrelated co-owners and for-sale housing.

Can a tenancy in common interest be inherited?
Yes. Because there is no right of survivorship, a tenant in common's interest passes through their estate to their heirs or beneficiaries. This is one of the reasons the structure suits unrelated buyers who want an inheritable asset.

How do tenants in common hold title in California?
A California deed to two or more unmarried people is presumed to create a tenancy in common unless it expressly states otherwise; joint tenancy must be stated. In a structured TIC project the percentages, occupancy rights and transfer rules are set out in a written TIC agreement rather than left to the default.

Sources and Review

This article describes general California practice for tenancy-in-common ownership and small-multifamily conversion. Subdivision requirements arise under the California Subdivision Map Act; conversion, tenant-protection, and rent-stabilization rules are set by state law and by individual jurisdictions, and Los Angeles imposes requirements beyond the state baseline. Fractional TIC lending terms are set by individual portfolio lenders and change with the market.

This is general information about California real estate practice, not legal, tax, or lending advice. Rules differ by jurisdiction and building and are amended regularly. Confirm current requirements with the local agency, a qualified California real estate attorney, and a lender before relying on anything described here.
